evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# @automagik/acp-dsh

Agents other than DSH's own, as DeepSeek Harness models, over the
[Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) (ACP). The design is
[RFC 0003](../../docs/rfcs/0003-model-routes-and-acp.md).

- **Agents as DSH models.** Each agent is a provider route (`acp-<agent>`) whose models are the
  agent's own (Claude Code's Opus, Sonnet, Haiku…; Codex's GPT models), each with the reasoning
  efforts the agent offers for it. A chat or a Bot picks one like any model. DSH keeps the
  Session, its history and the sidebar.
- **The agent's own models and efforts.** They are read from the agent over ACP: its session
  config options of category `model` and `thought_level`. A probe starts the adapter, opens a
  session it never prompts (no turn, no tokens), reads the models, then picks each one to read
  its efforts, since an agent rebuilds that list per model. The result is kept in
  `$AUTOMAGIK_HOME/acp/catalog/<route>.json`, so the next start lists it at once while a new probe
  runs; a new adapter release probes again. Before any probe has answered, a short list stands
  in (Claude Code: `default`, `opus`, `sonnet`, `haiku` at low, medium or high effort; Codex:
  `default`). The model `default` is always listed: it is whatever the agent's own settings
  choose. An effort's default is the person's own setting for that model.
- **The Session's model and effort, before each prompt.** The agent's session is put on the
  Session's model, then its effort (the model first: the efforts are that model's). No effort
  leaves the agent's own. A model or effort the agent does not offer fails the turn, naming what
  it offers.
- **DSH tool cards and approvals.** With `dshTools` off (the kill switch), the agent runs its own
  tools. Each tool call it makes ends the model step with a call to `acp_tool`, a tool registered
  in that agent's scope only. DSH writes the `tool/call` and `tool/result` rows and draws the
  card (a terminal for a command, a diff for an edit, the generic card otherwise). When the agent
  asks permission for the call, `acp_tool` asks DSH's approval service
  (`approval/asked`, `approval/decided`) and gives the agent DSH's answer. On DSH's Auto
  review level that answer is the review. A call the reviewer allowed, or that the person
  allowed in the dialog the reviewer raised, gets `allow_once` for the agent's first question
  about it, with no second dialog; this holds in a subagent child too. These still ask as before:
  a later question, a call the agent changed after its review (in its question or after it), an
  agent that offers no `allow_once`, and a level that changed since the call.
- **DSH's own tools over the bridge (`dshTools`).** On, the agent gets the Session's preset tool
  set (standard, or cordis in creator mode) over one stdio MCP server per ACP session, named
  `dsh` and spawned by the adapter with that session's arguments. The bridge has no port; it
  reaches this plugin over a loopback back-channel with a per-session credential
  (`DSH_BRIDGE_CREDENTIAL`), which binds a request to its Session and is revoked with the
  bridge. Every DSH tool call is approved in DSH under the Session's level before it runs,
  whatever the agent's own allow rules or hooks say, and the bridge writes the `tool/call` and
  `tool/result` rows the chat shows. `acp-claude` runs with its built-in tools off
  (`_meta.disableBuiltInTools`); a structured call that is not an MCP name is recorded as
  `plugin:acp-dsh/toolset-drift` and its turn is cancelled — the detector runs at every session
  start, and it detects and cancels because the update arrives after the call began.
  DSH's `read_image` works for Claude Code because acp-dsh declares its models as taking images;
  other ACP agents keep no declaration.
  `acp-codex` has no such switch, so it is bridged only with an explicit `dshTools: true`;
  absent or `false` means no bridge and its built-ins stay its own tool set. Until a structured
  name is proven in its tool calls, it draws no ACP card for an MCP call. The person's
  own MCP servers load beside the bridge with their own tools and sign-ins: DSH hands the session
  only the `dsh` bridge, so any other `mcp__<server>__<tool>` is the CLI's own user-scope config
  (claude-agent-acp merges the person's settings MCP servers into the session), it passes the
  drift allowlist by design, and DSH's Auto review does not gate it: the agent's own rules and
  sign-in govern that call. A tool-list change
  (a preset or level change) is announced on `acp-claude` and arrives through `session/fork`
  plus `session/close` on `acp-codex`; a bridge that never lists its tools fails the turn
  (`acp_bridge_missing`) before the prompt. **Auto:** DSH's Auto preset is full access's sandbox
  with asks answered by auto-review. A bridge call adds one marked, tool-only assistant block:
  the advertisement the Session format requires before its tool/call row, which the reviewer
  reads too, and which is removed from the surface once the call settles and never replayed to
  another provider; the reviewer sees the bridge tool, its redacted arguments and its schema
  before the body runs. A denial is `AUTO_REVIEW_DENIED`, a failed reviewer refuses with
  `AUTO_REVIEW_FAILED`, a review past its deadline is `AUTO_REVIEW_TIMEOUT`, and the call never
  runs. A call that comes between two steps of a turn while the agent's prompt is still running
  (after a `step/end`, before the next `step/start`) waits for the next step, at most 30 s, and is
  recorded and reviewed there; it ends with no rows if the turn ends, its caller goes away, the
  bridge is revoked or the turn is stopped (#969). Otherwise a Manual or Full call with no open
  step is `BRIDGE_NO_STEP` (Auto: `AUTO_REVIEW_NO_STEP`); one whose advertisement or
  call row cannot be written is `BRIDGE_RECORD_FAILED`, and the call does not run. The rows' call
  id is the agent's own `_meta.callId` only when it is 1 to 128 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ . : -`
  and does not start with `acp_` (the mirror's ids); otherwise the plugin mints `bridge_<16 hex>`
  and logs the replacement. **Codex's MCP approvals.** With `dshTools` on, `acp-codex`'s MCP calls
  get no mirror card (it gives them no structured name), so a `session/request_permission` Codex
  sends for one (codex-acp's MCP tool approval) is answered at once: allow once for the `dsh`
  server (the bridge's own approval is the one dialog), the agent's reject option for any other
  or unnamed server, which is logged (#969). **A call that
  outlives its step (#957).** The agent runs its calls in parallel, and the bridge puts no
  deadline on one (a long wait, a slow command and an open approval dialog are legitimate).
  Before its step ends, an own-tool card waits for bridge calls of that step asking for approval
  or under Auto review to write their results, with no deadline; Full-access calls are unchanged.
  Stop, revoke and the prompt's end release the wait.
  The write guard still closes calls a forced boundary leaves open before `step/end` and drops
  their late results; the agent still gets the real answer.
  Each call has its own abort controller: Stop, the end of its turn and a caller that
  went away (an MCP `notifications/cancelled`, a closed request) stop that call as
  `BRIDGE_CANCELLED` and keep the bridge. A call whose `tool/call` row cannot be written is
  answered with DSH's own not-started row, and a bridge revoked with a call in flight keeps
  the guard until that call is over. The reviewer
  goes to the same non-agent side model as a Session title. Manual asks (one dialog), Full
  access does not. A Session that moves between providers carries its transcript
  redacted at each crossing — the replay out to an agent, and the transcript handed back to a
  native provider — and each crossing writes a provider-boundary row the chat shows,
  "Switching to X": it is written before the reply and claims no answer, since the call can
  still fail after it. An agent whose CLI is signed out (ACP's `auth_required`, when its session
  opens or on a prompt) fails the turn as `MODEL_ACCESS_REQUIRED`, not `ACP_AGENT`. The
  reasoning effort the Session ran on crosses with it, both ways, when the target model offers
  that level (matched by id, else by name), replacing the target default DSH records on a model
  change; an effort DSH itself defaulted is not carried. The agents' levels are their own
  `thought_level` ids: Claude Code lists low, medium, high, xhigh and max, and Codex lists low,
  medium, high, xhigh, max and ultra, per model. A target with no reasoning levels, without
  that one, or whose levels cannot be read writes a notice row saying so and runs on its own.
  A switch back before the agent has answered drops the agent's chosen level; the native
  target's own default applies.
- **Only the chat reaches the agent.** DSH's side requests on an ACP route never become
  prompts. At the `llm/stream` waterfall a Session title (`purpose: session-title`) goes to a
  model that answers on its own, without the agent's effort. That is the first model the team
  can reach: DSH's default model (`agentDefaultModel`) when it is not an agent; else a
  `sideModel` the person chose; else each configured non-agent route in turn (its first model,
  at most eight); and only then the built-in DeepSeek Flash fallback. A credential or
  missing-route failure on one candidate moves to the next, so a team without a DeepSeek key
  reviews and titles on the model it does have; only no answer at all refuses. Auto review
  (`purpose: auto-review`) takes the same route, with its messages redacted first. Every other
  side request on an ACP route, a compaction summary included, is refused (`UNSUPPORTED`): it
  would carry the agent's whole chat to another provider, and the agent manages its own context.
  Sessions on any other route are left alone.
- **A switch onto an agent passes DSH's compaction guard.** `compaction-basic` prices every model
  switch on the destination's context window, which an agent does not declare, so a switch onto
  an agent in a Session with a request header used to fail with `MODEL_SWITCH_COMPACTION_FAILED`.
  This plugin wraps the engine's `compactPressure` (`src/host/pressure.js`, the method's only
  Automagik owner): an agent destination needs no compaction, every other destination goes to the
  engine unchanged. The wrapper is adopted when an agent is created and on its requests (a
  reloaded compaction plugin is a new engine), delegates to whatever is below it at call time, and
  on dispose unwinds only when it is on top. The method is private to `compaction-basic`; a guard
  test pins it, and a DSH flag for it is proposed upstream (RFC 0023). A switch *off* an agent is
  the destination's own business: for a Bot, the Bot team decides before the guard (its README,
  "Long chats").
- **Host only.** No browser half, so the plugin cannot stop the web UI from loading. With no
  agent CLI installed it registers no route. The welcome draws its setup from the `acpAgents`
  service below.
- **The Session's level, as the agent's own mode.** Before each prompt the agent's ACP session
  mode follows the Session: Manual is Claude Code's `default` mode, whatever default mode its
  own settings name; Codex runs in the sandbox that matches DSH's. DSH Auto review is Claude Code's `auto`
  and Codex's `agent`; it is the preset's identity, never just its sandbox and ask, so a custom
  preset with the same knobs keeps Manual (and the bridge's own approval). Full access lets every
  call through, as it does DSH's own tools. An agent that does not offer the strict mode fails
  the turn instead of running in its own default.
  A Workspace Session on unbridged Codex can instead take `agent` when the Bot team's
  `ownMode` answerer returns exactly `true` twice, before the prompt. After that agent session
  has attempted the own mode, any Workspace prompt that does not take it re-sends and confirms
  strict `workspace-write` (or its chat profile below), even if cached; refusal ends the agent
  session and fails the turn.
  Sessions that never attempt the own mode keep the usual mode cache and failure handling.
  Auto never requests `bypassPermissions` or
  `agent-full-access`. Codex's own reviewer decides those steps, based on the
  [Codex 0.167.0 capture](test/fixtures/permission-payloads/README.md); later versions may
  decide differently. Any approval Codex still requests goes to the person.
- **An agent that stops answering never holds the chat.** Its start (`initialize`,
  `session/new`, the bridge's first list) has 60 seconds, and each request after that and
  before a prompt (a model, an effort, a mode, a fork, a close) has 15. Past the deadline, or
  on Stop, the agent's process and its bridge are ended and the turn says what happened. A
  start that hangs is usually a CLI waiting for the person (a first-run question, a keychain
  dialog, an update), so that message says to open it once in a terminal. Stop ends the turn
  at once and gives the agent 5 seconds to end its prompt, because `session/cancel` is only a
  notification. An agent that ignores it is ended, and the next message starts a new agent
  session with the chat replayed to it (with `dshTools: false`, the new-session notice
  instead). A message sent while the agent is still on its last prompt waits those 5 seconds,
  then gets a new session in the same turn. Ending an agent ends what it started too (the
  command behind a stuck tool call): the agent leads its own process group, which is asked to
  end and killed 3 seconds later if any of it is left; on Windows its process tree is killed.
- **Claude Code keeps the person's own settings.** It loads their Claude Code settings (user,
  project and local) and asks DSH only for what those leave as "ask". A call their allow rules,
  saved "always allow" rules or PreToolUse/PermissionRequest hooks approve runs with no DSH
  dialog. This is the owner's decision (RFC 0003, Decided).

## Agents

Unbridged Claude Code receives per-session ask rules for recursive deletion, destructive Git,
infrastructure and database shell commands at every asking level. These explicit rules also
ask in Claude's auto mode. They are never written to a CLI home and are absent at Full access,
where explicit ask rules would otherwise still ask. Crossing Full access restarts the unbridged
Claude session with the chat replayed, adding or removing the rules; staying at a level reuses it.
Bridged Claude has its built-in tools disabled, so DSH checks its calls instead.

Codex's own tools are excluded: prompt rules under Full access (`approval_policy = never`)
refuse rather than ask, its session-flags configuration has no rules folder, and in `agent`
mode prompt rules reach Codex's reviewer rather than the person. Replacing its entire reviewer
policy or changing codex-acp needs a separate owner decision.

| Route | Agent | Runs | Adapter (newest release) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `acp-claude` | Claude Code | managed or existing `claude` (`CLAUDE_CODE_EXECUTABLE`) | `@agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp` |
| `acp-codex` | Codex | managed or existing `codex` (`CODEX_PATH`) | `@agentclientprotocol/codex-acp` |
| `acp-hermes` | Hermes | existing `hermes`, started as `hermes acp` | none: the CLI is the ACP server |
| `acp-antigravity` | Antigravity | existing `agy`, started as `agy acp` | none: the CLI is the ACP server |
| `acp-omp` | omp | existing `omp`, started as `omp acp` | none: the CLI is the ACP server |
| `acp-fake` | `dev/fake-agent.mjs`, set as `fakeAgent` | Node | none; tests only |

An agent is offered when its managed CLI is ready, or an existing CLI is on PATH or where its
installer puts it (`~/.local/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin`, …). The settings `claude: false` or `codex: false` take one away;
`hermes`, `antigravity` and `omp` are off until set to `true` (below). They are
live settings: switching one (from the welcome's Connect AI, its Settings page *Claude Code and
Codex*, or the plugin's own settings form) offers or withdraws the agent at once, with no
restart, and a connector that lands puts its model in the picker the same way
(`llm/adapters-updated`).

### Native-ACP agents: Hermes, Antigravity, omp

These three speak ACP themselves, so there is no adapter package and nothing is installed for
them: the plugin starts the CLI it finds with `acp` (`src/host/agents.js`, `launch`). What
differs from Claude Code and Codex:

- **Off until turned on.** `hermes`, `antigravity` and `omp` are live settings that default to
  `false`. Turning one on is the person's word that Automagik may use the sign-in that CLI
  already has on this computer, shared with their terminal. No account is read for them (none
  of the three has a command that names one), so the account record and its confirm step
  (below) stay Claude Code's and Codex's.
- **Never installed by Automagik.** A CLI that is not here is listed as missing with its
  install page (`cli.state: 'missing'`, `connector.state: 'no-cli'`), never hidden and never
  "installing". Once found, the connector reads `ready` with `native: true`.
- **Sign-in in a terminal.** There is no sign-in from a Bot's chat: `loginStart` refuses with
  `acp-login/terminal` and the command (`hermes acp --setup`, `agy acp --login`, `omp login`),
  and a signed-out turn fails as `MODEL_ACCESS_REQUIRED` naming the same command. Whether the
  agent is signed in is what its own ACP session said: `true` when the session the model read
  opens, `false` on ACP's `auth_required`. That read runs when the CLI changes and once a day,
  and again when the person asks (`refresh()`) while it is not signed in; no other check opens
  a session, because each of these agents keeps every session it opens in its own history.
  A session that opens does not prove a provider key works: a turn that then answers
  `auth_required` reads as signed out at once.
- **Models.** Antigravity offers its models and efforts as config options, as the adapters do.
  Hermes offers them only as the session's own list (`models` in the `session/new` answer,
  switched with `session/set_model`); the plugin reads that list when the agent has no model
  option. omp offers no model list over ACP: it is one model, `default`, its own setting.
- **The level.** Each is put in its own `default` mode before every prompt, whatever the
  Session's level, and what it asks is answered by DSH's approval under that level. Its own
  permission settings still decide what it asks about. One that does not offer `default`
  fails the turn. A table agent with no mode for DSH's level would say so once in the chat.
- **No DSH tool bridge.** DSH's tools do not reach them, even with `dshTools: true`: their
  tool naming over ACP is not proven the way Claude Code's was, and an unrecognised bridge
  call would draw two cards and ask twice. They keep their own tools; the transcript replay on
  a model switch reaches them like any agent.

`dshTools` (live, no schema default) is the bridge, its DSH approval, the drift detector and live
switching above. Absent means the per-agent default: `acp-claude` bridges because its adapter can
drop its own built-in tools; `acp-codex` does not, because it cannot. Codex is bridged only with
an explicit `true`; absent or `false` means no bridge, and Codex keeps its own built-in tools as
its only tool set. An explicit `false` is the kill switch for Claude too: the 2026-11-03
behaviour, where each agent keeps its own tools and its own approvals. The key is public and
stays writable through
DSH's settings service or the profile patch, but it is hidden from settings forms (`.hidden()`):
it is a rollback lever, not a preference. Flipping it either way ends the running agent sessions
and revokes their bridges at once; the DSH Session keeps its transcript and the next turn starts
afresh under the new setting. A flip is also announced on the plugin context as
`acp-dsh/dsh-tools-changed` with `{ on }`: DSH delivers `loader/volatile-update` only to the
plugin whose config changed, so another plugin would never see this one. The Bot team watches
that event, so turning the switch off moves its Claude Bots back at once, and turning it on moves
them again. A listener that throws is logged as a warning; the flip itself and its ended sessions
still hold, and the Bot team reverses at its next start (the route reads off or gone). The default
moves Claude Bots once per team to `acp-claude` (the Bot team's README,
"Claude on ACP"); the bridge probe in `bridge()` still gates the move.

The transcript replay is independent of the bridge: only an explicit `false` turns it off.

| `dshTools` | Claude Code: tools | Claude Code: replay | Codex: tools | Codex: replay |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| absent | DSH bridge, its own off | yes | its own only | yes |
| `true` | DSH bridge | yes | DSH bridge and its own | yes |
| `false` | its own only | no | its own only | no |

So with `dshTools` absent Codex sees the chat but not the team's tools; those need an explicit
`true` (two tool sets). A replay reaches an agent in each of these cases, redacted and capped at
120,000 characters, the oldest messages dropped first with a marker: a move from another
provider (with its "Switching to X" row); a new agent session in a chat that already has answers
(after a restart, or a session a crossing or a flip ended), with no row since the chat stayed on
that agent; and a live session resumed after the chat answered elsewhere (a move off Codex keeps
its session), which gets only the turns it missed, from its own last answer on, with the row. A
Bot part's handoff package (a relay marked `handoff`) is carried as the record it is: in the
part's first turn it stays in the prompt beside the person's words, and once the Bot team has
answered that turn itself, the next new session gets it in the replay. Both pass the redactor.
With `false`, an agent sees only its own session, and a new one in a chat with answers writes the
"does not see this chat's earlier messages" row instead.

`sideModel` (`{ provider, model }`, default `deepseek-official/deepseek-flash`, live) is the
model a side request tries after DSH's default model. An explicit value the person chose is tried
before the configured non-agent routes (each in turn, its first model); the default DeepSeek
Flash is tried last, so a team without a DeepSeek key titles and reviews on the model it does
have. An agent route set here is ignored, and a credential or missing-route failure falls
through to the next candidate.

## The `acpAgents` service

A settings page reads the agents through this host service; the plugin stays host only.

| Method | Does |
|---|---|
| `status()` | Each agent: `{ id, key, name, on, cli: { found, installUrl, signInHint?, state, managed, version?, error?, diagnostic?, logPath?, updating? }, connector: { state, native?, version?, error?, diagnostic?, logPath?, updating?, startError?, previous?, rolledBack? }, signedIn?, signInCheck?, consent?, model: { provider, id, name, listed }, restartNeeded }`. CLI state is `missing`, `installing`, `failed` or `ready`; connector state is `off`, `no-cli`, `installing`, `failed` or `ready`. `connector.previous` is the release a failed start goes back to, while it is on disk; `connector.rolledBack` is `{ from, to, at, reason }` while a release that failed to start is held back. `connector.startError` is the short reason an installed connector's last start failed, until a session opens or Retry reinstalls it; a connector being reinstalled reads `installing`. A failed connector install always carries `error`; `diagnostic` (the end of the installer's output) and `logPath` (the file it was written to, shown from the home folder) are optional, as for a failed CLI install. `signedIn` is absent while the sign-in is unknown; `signInCheck` then says why the last check of the CLI's status command could not tell: `timeout` (the CLI was ended after 8 seconds) or `unreadable` (it could not be run, or answered something this does not read). Neither field: nothing is known of a check (none has run yet, or the agent has no status command: a native agent's sign-in comes from its own ACP session). Errors are redacted. Spawns nothing. |
| `inspect(id)` | One agent's `status()` row with a fresh sign-in check, for a Bot about to be put on it. Asks that CLI's sign-in status only; installs, enables and starts nothing. Simultaneous checks share one probe. An answer stands for 3 seconds, and a confirmed sign-in for 5 minutes, since the check starts the whole CLI; `refresh()` clears it, and so does the agent itself saying it is signed out (ACP `auth_required`). Undefined for an id that is no agent here. |
| `refresh()` | Looks for the CLIs again (one installed after DSH started is offered now), then asks each CLI whether it is signed in (`claude auth status --json`, of which only `loggedIn` is read; `codex login status`, by its exit code). No agent turn. |
| `retry(id)` | Retries the required CLI and its connector, and answers at once. A connector whose last start or install failed, or that is missing, is reinstalled at the release in use (below); else the connector is checked for a newer release. Does not turn its model switch on. |
| `loginStart(id, { label? })` | Starts the CLI's own sign-in (`src/host/login.js`), or answers the attempt already at work for that agent. Codex: a device code through `codex app-server`; Claude Code: `claude auth login --claudeai`, whose link must ask for the manual code (`code=true`). Only the official authorization pages are relayed. `label` names the view that opened it (a Bot id), for a cancel confirmation; it is not an access check. An attempt that fails writes one line to the host log: a fixed class (no CLI found, no sign-in link in time, unsupported sign-in link, the CLI exited, the CLI could not be started, the CLI did not confirm the sign-in, device-code login is not enabled, device sign-in did not start, or unknown), where the attempt stood, how the CLI ended, and the version the CLI had when the attempt started. Never what the CLI printed. |
| `loginCurrent(id)` | The attempt at work for that agent, from any view, or undefined. Never starts or cancels one. |
| `loginStatus(id, attemptId)` / `loginAnswer(id, attemptId, value)` / `loginCancel(id, attemptId)` | Reads an attempt (an ended one stays readable for 60 seconds), sends Claude's pasted `code#state` to the CLI (which then has 90 seconds to confirm), or ends it. |
| `loginTextMatches(text)` | Whether a text carries a Claude sign-in state shown in the last 24 hours. Only a boolean: the states are kept as keyed hashes in memory. |
| `loginActive()` | How many attempts are starting or waiting. |
| `account(id, { fresh? })` | For the DSH owner's views only: `{ id, signedIn?, consent?, ref?, account?: { kind: 'account' \| 'key', email?, org?, plan? }, notice? }`. Who the CLI is signed in as, read from the CLI itself (below); never on a `status()` or `inspect()` row, in a log or in an event. `ref` names the account read and goes back with `accountConfirm`. |
| `accountConfirm(id, { ref? })` | The person's word that the app may use the account this CLI is signed in to. Asks the CLI again, records the consent and announces `acp-dsh/login-ready`. Another account than `ref` is refused (`acp-account/changed`); a signed-out CLI too (`acp-account/signed-out`). |
| `accountNoticed(id)` | The one-time notice of a vendor carried through an upgrade was shown. |
| `imageAccess()` | `{ ready, signedIn?, reason?, unsupported? }`: whether Codex can draw an image now, on its own ChatGPT sign-in (Codex on, its CLI found, its connector installed, `codex login status` says signed in; an unknown sign-in is asked once; the person confirmed its account, else `reason: 'account'`; the image run's checks hold for this Codex, else not ready, with `reason`: `unsupported` (and `unsupported: true`), `config` or `unreadable`). Reads no credential and starts no sign-in. |
| `generateImage({ prompt, size?, quality?, background?, signal?, timeoutMs? })` | Draws one image with the Codex CLI (`src/host/image.js`) and resolves `{ base64, mimeType: 'image/png' }`. Refusals carry an `acp/image-*` code (`signed-out`, `usage-limit`, `timeout`, `unavailable`, `failed`, `stopped`, `refused`) and a message to show as it is. |
| `keepImages(keeper)` | Where an image an agent makes in a chat is kept, so the chat can show it (`src/host/agent-image.js`). `keeper` is `{ start?({ callId, sessionId, via }), keep({ callId, sessionId, base64, mimeType, via }) -> Promise<{ file }>, fail?({ callId, sessionId, error }) }`; one at a time, and the call returns its disposer. The Bot team registers its images folder. |
| `ownMode(answer)` | Registers one answerer for an unbridged Workspace Session's own mode. Only exact `true` within two seconds counts, twice per prompt. Returns a disposer for that registration; competing registrations disable own mode permanently. |
| `ownModeOf(provider)` | `{ mode, bridged, answerer }` for a provider offering its own mode, otherwise undefined. |
| `ownModeIn(sessionId)` | Whether that Session is busy on a prompt in its own mode. |
| `holdTurns(gate)` | A veto on agent turns, for a plugin that must keep an agent from acting in a Session (the Bot team: a Session whose permission level could not be set). `gate({ sessionId, agent, provider })` is asked before every model step on an agent's route and again right before a turn's prompt is sent; it answers undefined to let the Session go, or the sentence the step answers with. It can only refuse: a gate that throws, takes longer than ten seconds, or answers anything else holds the Session with a fixed sentence, and a held Session's agent session is ended. Several plugins may register: any refusal wins, and the returned disposer removes only its own gate. With none registered nothing is asked. |
| `endSession(sessionI

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
Automagik

A team of AI helpers that lives in your chats.

Automagik is superintelligence, in open building blocks: a team of AI agents in your chats,
and each part usable on its own once it ships; Cloud is still in design.

The film: our own GTM team. The team launching Automagik, at work. Music only, no voice-over.
Watch the film on automagik.si

⬇ Download for Mac  ·  ⬇ Download for Linux

Cloud is coming; no date yet. Join the Cloud waitlist on automagik.si

This repository, Genie and Omni are free and open source, Apache-2.0. Cloud is a private, paid service.
Mac with Apple silicon, macOS 13 or newer · Linux on a 64-bit PC · Windows is not supported yet

--- ## Two modes **Team mode** is the desktop app: a team of long-lived Bots, each with its own name, role, model and memory. They talk to you, to each other and in group chats, run scheduled tasks, and each drives a browser of its own. With an [Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni) connected, your WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack and other channels sit in the same window, and the Bot you put on a chat acts when something happens there. The team runs on [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH). **Code mode** is your code agents in the real [Herdr](https://herdr.dev) window, with the Automagik pack: a sidebar of spaces, Bots and workers across coding harnesses. Nothing in Herdr is rebuilt. The app's switch brings the Herdr window forward on the space for the current Bot's folder, and a button in Herdr brings you back. The app download alone does not set Code mode up: it needs Herdr and the pack, and [the pack's installer](herdr/README.md#install) sets up both. Team mode: the app's switch still says Work. ## The seven blocks Each block is usable alone. - **[Team mode (DSH)](apps/bots-dsh/README.md)**: the Bot team on DeepSeek Harness: long-lived Bots with their own name, role, model and memory, group chats, schedules and the Bot browser. - **[Code mode (Herdr)](herdr/README.md)**: your code agents in the real Herdr window with the Automagik pack; nothing in Herdr is rebuilt. - **[Genie](https://github.com/automagik-si/genie)**: a wish becomes a branch, a test run and a report you approve; `genie desktop` opens it on the team. - **[Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni)**: the service that links your chat apps to Automagik, with its channels and canvases in the same window. - **[Pocket](apps/pocket/README.md)**: your coding agents on your Android phone, paired to your own machines. - **[The meter](meter/usagemeter/README.md)**: usagemeter, the Rust token meter that records usage and cost on the machine and answers `usagemeter query`. - **[Cloud](docs/rfcs/0024-automagik-cloud.md)**: one sign-in, organisations and hosted workspaces, with a rail that opens each. Cloud is designed and accepted, and is not live. When it ships it is a private, paid hosted service: not free and not open source. Only its contracts are public (RFC 0024). ## What makes it yours - **Your model.** Connect the AI account you already have, or an API key from a provider you use. Each Bot runs on the model you give it. - **Your files and memory, on your computer.** What the team keeps is in one folder, `.automagik` in your home folder. Each Bot keeps notes across its conversations, each group chat keeps its own, and the team shares one more. Your chats stay in your Omni. What your Bots read and write goes to the AI account you connected, under that company's terms. - **Secrets the Bots never see.** When a Bot needs an API key, a token or a password, it asks with a card in its own chat. You type the value; the Bot never sees it. - **It asks before it acts as you.** Before a Bot sends a message as you to a person, deletes something or disconnects a channel, it shows you exactly what it will do and asks first. The exceptions: your Main Bot and an Omni Bot read your chats and post to a group, a WhatsApp channel or your own chat with yourself without asking. Any other Bot reads and posts only where you allow: the first time it wants a chat it asks, and you answer **Once**, **Always** or **No**; after **Always** it posts to that group without asking again. ## Install The current release is always at [Releases](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest). **Mac** (Apple silicon, macOS 13 or newer): 1. [Download Automagik for Mac](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest/download/Automagik-Mac.dmg). 2. Open **Automagik-Mac.dmg** and drag the Automagik icon onto the Applications folder. 3. Open **Automagik** from Applications. **Linux** (64-bit PC): 1. [Download Automagik for Linux (.deb)](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest/download/Automagik-Linux.deb) for Ubuntu or Debian. 2. Double-click it and choose **Install**, or run `sudo apt install ./Automagik-Linux.deb`. 3. Open **Automagik** from your apps. On another Linux, use the [AppImage](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest/download/Automagik-Linux.AppImage). Windows is not supported yet. The app has two things to connect when you are ready: an Omni and an AI account. Both can wait. The full guide, updates, your data and uninstall are in [apps/desktop](apps/desktop/README.md). Code mode installs separately: [herdr](herdr/README.md#install). Pocket: [apps/pocket](apps/pocket/README.md#install). **For your code agent**: `npx skills add automagik-si/automagik --skill am` adds the skill that teaches it `am`, Automagik's one command. ## This repository Automagik's plugins for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH), and the Automagik desktop app that runs them, with the Herdr pack (`herdr/`), Pocket (`apps/pocket/`) and the meter (`meter/`). | Folder | Package | What it is | |---|---|---| | [`apps/bots-dsh`](apps/bots-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/bots-dsh` | The Bot team: long-lived Bots, group chats, memory, settings, scheduled tasks, the Bot browser. Omni's and Genie's plugins build on it. | | [`apps/welcome-dsh`](apps/welcome-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/welcome-dsh` | The welcome: the octopus, the team step, and Connect AI through DSH's own sign-ins. | | [`apps/acp-dsh`](apps/acp-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/acp-dsh` | Agents other than DSH's own, over ACP (Agent Client Protocol), as DSH models: the agent's tool calls show as DSH tool cards and ask through DSH's approval dialog (RFC 0003). | | [`apps/locale-pt-br-dsh`](apps/locale-pt-br-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/locale-pt-br-dsh` | Português: the Bot team's Brazilian Portuguese under DSH's own Portuguese entry. Adds no language of its own, so Settings › General › Language keeps one Portuguese row; a pt-BR choice saved by an older pack moves to DSH's pt. | | [`apps/desktop`](apps/desktop/README.md) | (the app) | The Automagik desktop app: DSH of its own with the Bot team, the welcome and Omni's channels and canvases. `omni desktop` opens it with Omni preloaded, `genie desktop` with Genie. | Omni's own plugins (its channels and canvases) live with Omni, in [automagik-si/omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni) (`apps/omni-channels-dsh`, `apps/omni-canvas-dsh`), and carry Omni's version. ### Install into your own DSH - **The desktop app**: download it from [Releases](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest), or run `omni desktop`. See [apps/desktop](apps/desktop/README.md). - **Into your own DSH**: add the Automagik market to DSH's plugin market and install from there: ``` https://raw.githubusercontent.com/automagik-si/dsh-marketplace/main/index.json ``` Every Omni also serves a market at `https:///api/market/index.json` with the release of these plugins it was tested with. Nothing here is published to npm. The plugins install as git sources pinned to a release commit, or from the tarballs each release carries (`plugins.json` lists their integrity). ### History `@automagik/bots-dsh` and `@automagik/welcome-dsh` were `@automagik/omni-dsh` and `@automagik/omni-ai-dsh` in automagik-dev/omni (`apps/omni-ui-dsh`, `apps/omni-ai-dsh`), and the desktop app was automagik-dev/omni-desktop. They moved here with their history. What did not change with the names: plugin ids (`omni-ui`, `omni-ai`), routes and browser-storage prefixes. From 3.12 the team's home is Automagik's own (`~/.automagik/bots`, or `~/.automagik/desktop/bots` in the app), and the app's identity is Automagik's (`ai.namastex.automagik`): an app from 3.11.x or before is installed afresh, not updated. - The Bot team's client bundle also answers to its former name, so channels and canvas plugins built before the rename keep working on it. - In your own DSH: install `@automagik/bots-dsh` from the market. With both installed, the newer one runs (they share the plugin id); remove `@automagik/omni-dsh` when you like. A settings row in your profile's `cordis.patch.yml` that names `@automagik/omni-dsh` needs its `name:` changed to `@automagik/bots-dsh` to keep applying. ### Versions and releases One version for the whole repository, `3.N` (semver `3.N.0`, N one above the last release: `scripts/version.ts`), above the 2.x builds omni-desktop released. Every merge into dev is a release: `release.yml` tags `v`, publishes the plugin tarballs and `plugins.json`, builds the desktop app into the same release (`desktop-build.yml`), lists the release in [`marketplace/automagik.json`](marketplace/automagik.json), and moves `main` to it. `follow-omni.yml` moves the desktop app to each newer Omni release and cuts a release with it. | Branch | What | |---|---| | `dev` | Integration: pull requests land here; releases are cut from it | | `main` | The latest release, moved by `release.yml` only | ### Develop Bun for the repository's own tooling; the plugins run on Node, as DSH does (`node --test`, esbuild), with Bun installing them; the desktop app uses npm for Electron. ```sh bun install && bun run check # versions, release tooling, market index cd apps/bots-dsh && bun install && bun run harness && bun run test cd apps/welcome-dsh && bun install && bun run harness && bun run test cd apps/desktop && npm ci && npm test node scripts/boot-check.mjs # boot the plugins with Omni's in headless Chromium ``` ### License This repository is Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE). [Genie](https://github.com/automagik-si/genie) and [Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni) are Apache-2.0 in their own repositories. Automagik Cloud is not part of this licence: it is a private, paid service.

Pocket: [apps/pocket](apps/pocket/README.md#install). **For your code agent**: `npx skills add automagik-si/automagik --skill am` adds the skill that teaches it `am`, Automagik's one command. ## This repository Automagik's plugins for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (DSH), and the Automagik desktop app that runs them, with the Herdr pack (`herdr/`), Pocket (`apps/pocket/`) and the meter (`meter/`). | Folder | Package | What it is | |---|---|---| | [`apps/bots-dsh`](apps/bots-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/bots-dsh` | The Bot team: long-lived Bots, group chats, memory, settings, scheduled tasks, the Bot browser. Omni's and Genie's plugins build on it. | | [`apps/welcome-dsh`](apps/welcome-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/welcome-dsh` | The welcome: the octopus, the team step, and Connect AI through DSH's own sign-ins. | | [`apps/acp-dsh`](apps/acp-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/acp-dsh` | Agents other than DSH's own, over ACP (Agent Client Protocol), as DSH models: the agent's tool calls show as DSH tool cards and ask through DSH's approval dialog (RFC 0003). | | [`apps/locale-pt-br-dsh`](apps/locale-pt-br-dsh/README.md) | `@automagik/locale-pt-br-dsh` | Português: the Bot team's Brazilian Portuguese under DSH's own Portuguese entry. Adds no language of its own, so Settings › General › Language keeps one Portuguese row; a pt-BR choice saved by an older pack moves to DSH's pt. | | [`apps/desktop`](apps/desktop/README.md) | (the app) | The Automagik desktop app: DSH of its own with the Bot team, the welcome and Omni's channels and canvases. `omni desktop` opens it with Omni preloaded, `genie desktop` with Genie. | Omni's own plugins (its channels and canvases) live with Omni, in [automagik-si/omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni) (`apps/omni-channels-dsh`, `apps/omni-canvas-dsh`), and carry Omni's version. ### Install into your own DSH - **The desktop app**: download it from [Releases](https://github.com/automagik-si/automagik/releases/latest), or run `omni desktop`. See [apps/desktop](apps/desktop/README.md). - **Into your own DSH**: add the Automagik market to DSH's plugin market and install from there: ``` https://raw.githubusercontent.com/automagik-si/dsh-marketplace/main/index.json ``` Every Omni also serves a market at `https:///api/market/index.json` with the release of these plugins it was tested with. Nothing here is published to npm. The plugins install as git sources pinned to a release commit, or from the tarballs each release carries (`plugins.json` lists their integrity). ### History `@automagik/bots-dsh` and `@automagik/welcome-dsh` were `@automagik/omni-dsh` and `@automagik/omni-ai-dsh` in automagik-dev/omni (`apps/omni-ui-dsh`, `apps/omni-ai-dsh`), and the desktop app was automagik-dev/omni-desktop. They moved here with their history. What did not change with the names: plugin ids (`omni-ui`, `omni-ai`), routes and browser-storage prefixes. From 3.12 the team's home is Automagik's own (`~/.automagik/bots`, or `~/.automagik/desktop/bots` in the app), and the app's identity is Automagik's (`ai.namastex.automagik`): an app from 3.11.x or before is installed afresh, not updated. - The Bot team's client bundle also answers to its former name, so channels and canvas plugins built before the rename keep working on it. - In your own DSH: install `@automagik/bots-dsh` from the market. With both installed, the newer one runs (they share the plugin id); remove `@automagik/omni-dsh` when you like. A settings row in your profile's `cordis.patch.yml` that names `@automagik/omni-dsh` needs its `name:` changed to `@automagik/bots-dsh` to keep applying. ### Versions and releases One version for the whole repository, `3.N` (semver `3.N.0`, N one above the last release: `scripts/version.ts`), above the 2.x builds omni-desktop released. Every merge into dev is a release: `release.yml` tags `v`, publishes the plugin tarballs and `plugins.json`, builds the desktop app into the same release (`desktop-build.yml`), lists the release in [`marketplace/automagik.json`](marketplace/automagik.json), and moves `main` to it. `follow-omni.yml` moves the desktop app to each newer Omni release and cuts a release with it. | Branch | What | |---|---| | `dev` | Integration: pull requests land here; releases are cut from it | | `main` | The latest release, moved by `release.yml` only | ### Develop Bun for the repository's own tooling; the plugins run on Node, as DSH does (`node --test`, esbuild), with Bun installing them; the desktop app uses npm for Electron. ```sh bun install && bun run check # versions, release tooling, market index cd apps/bots-dsh && bun install && bun run harness && bun run test cd apps/welcome-dsh && bun install && bun run harness && bun run test cd apps/desktop && npm ci && npm test node scripts/boot-check.mjs # boot the plugins with Omni's in headless Chromium ``` ### License This repository is Apache-2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) and [NOTICE](NOTICE). [Genie](https://github.com/automagik-si/genie) and [Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni) are Apache-2.0 in their own repositories. evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# @automagik/bots-dsh

Omni for [DeepSeek Harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness) (dsh): a team of long-lived Bots that talk to you, to each other and in group chats, with Omni as the Main Bot. With the Omni channels plugin, Omni also operates your Omni channels, chats and automations inside dsh; with the Omni canvas plugin, it shows what it found as live views in the chat (see [Three plugins](#three-plugins)). It is built on [DS Bot](https://github.com/Fei2411/DeepSeek-Bot) (Apache-2.0, see `VENDORED.md`).

> Labs release. Features, tools and the saved data format can still change.

The dsh versions it supports are the range in `engines.dsh` in its [`package.json`](package.json); dsh checks that range and does not load the plugin on a version outside it.

**Your own dsh stays yours.** Installed into an existing dsh, the team keeps its files in `$AUTOMAGIK_HOME/bots` (`~/.automagik/bots`), keeps the key of the Omni it is linked to in its own file there, uses its own route (`/api/omni-ui`), plugin id (`omni-ui`) and browser-storage prefix (`omni-ui:`), overrides no other plugin's configuration, and checks for no updates. It can run beside upstream DS Bot.

## Three plugins

Omni for dsh is three packages. This one is the team; the other two sit on it and add Omni's own parts. Install all three to have everything; the team works alone.

| Package | Folder | Row id | What it adds |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@automagik/bots-dsh` (this one) | `apps/bots-dsh` | `omni-ui` | The Bot team and its surface: Bots, group chats, settings, themes, interface copy, memory, secrets, usage, scheduled tasks, the Bot browser, updates, diagnostics, the `POST /api/omni-ui` route, and the `web-search` plugin |
| `@automagik/omni-channels-dsh` | [`apps/omni-channels-dsh` in Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni/tree/dev/apps/omni-channels-dsh#readme) | `omni-channels` | The link to an Omni (pairing, `omni.json`), the Channels page and chats, Omni's tools for the platform (and the shell and file tools a Main Bot loses for them), the events Omni listens to, automations and their board, Omni's operator rules, and the onboarding step Connect Omni (`omni-connect`) |
| `@automagik/omni-canvas-dsh` | [`apps/omni-canvas-dsh` in Omni](https://github.com/automagik-si/omni/tree/dev/apps/omni-canvas-dsh#readme) | `omni-canvas` | `show_canvas`, the canvas check, the canvas language in Omni's rules, and the renderer that draws canvases in the chat (OpenUI and zod live only here) |

How they fit:

- **Host**: this plugin provides its runtime as the `omniTeam` service. The channels plugin injects it, installs its modules on a runtime whose prototype is the team's, and provides that one as `omniChannels`; the canvas plugin injects both and sits on the channels runtime. Each plugin's tools, listeners and effects stay on its own fiber, and it adds to the team only through `rt.hooks` (`src/host/extend.js`): `endpoint(name, fn, { read })` for the `/api/omni-ui` route, `view(fn)` and `live(fn)` for the state answers, `sessionOwner(fn)` for the team Bot and optional label of an external run Session, and `mainRules(fn, { order })` for a part of the Main Bot's rules, which stay inside the one `bot-identity` section. A plugin that runs a Bot kind on its own engine, not on a DSH model, owns that kind's model menu with `botModels(kind, { snapshot, pick, refresh })` (`src/host/host-models.js` has the shape): the team then never selects a DSH model for those Bots (their settings and `list_bots` name what the plugin says answers), their menu lists only the plugin's entries (each with where a message goes, the one picked and the one answering now) and levels, and only you pick; a Bot's `update_bot` with a model or level is refused. Without a registration the team answers as before. Each hook returns its disposer, so turning a plugin off takes what it added with it. Five more parts of the runtime are for other plugins:
  - `rt.resumable.register({ id, sessions, onResume })` hands the team's one restart pass (`src/host/resume.js`) the plain Sessions a plugin owns: `sessions()` names them when the pass runs, `onResume({ sessionId })` runs right before the team posts a resume to one of them (whoever found it), and the registration returns its disposer. Every resume post carries `source.resumed === true`.
  - `rt.resumesDone` is one promise per start that never rejects: `{ resumed, resent }` after the pass, `{ readOnly, resumed: [], resent: [] }` on a host that only reads the team, `{ failed, resumed, resent }` when it threw or stopped. `resumed` lists every Session the pass resumed, `resent` every Session it sent dropped messages again.
  - `rt.noteStop(sessionId, { why, tool, callId, text })` notes a permission stop for the person; `rt.teamOwnerOf(sessionId, agent)` resolves the team Bot and place, including a subagent's parent. Plugins can feature-detect both. Reasons are `never`, `unavailable`, `tool`, `level`, `address`, `review`, `sandbox` and `rule`; external grants and guards use `rule`.
  - `rt.dshBots`: `list()` gives `[{ id, name, workDir, profile }]` (`null`: the team workspace, DSH's default preset), `createSession(botId, { title, firstMessage })` gives `{ sessionId }` in that DSH bot's folder with its preset, and `onChange(fn)` calls `fn(list)` when the list changes and returns its disposer.
  - `rt.mountCapability(sessionId, name, grant)` and `rt.unmountCapability(sessionId, name)` mount one MCP capability into one plain Session the plugin owns, and only there ([A capability for one Session](#a-capability-for-one-session)).
- **Browser**: this plugin's `client.js` exports `omni`: the host call, the interface copy (`t`, `addStrings`), the Bot surface's registries (`toolCards`, `nav`, `badges`, `botChildren`, `headerButtons`, `sidebarTools`, `botSettings`, `onShell`, `setCanvasRenderer`, `registerComposerPack`), the running surface (`face`) and a few UI pieces (`ui`). The other plugins name `@automagik/bots-dsh/client` in `dsh.client.external`, so dsh loads this bundle first and hands them the same module instance: one dictionary, one roster, one set of registries.
- **Composer**: a Bot's composer changes with the model it runs on (`src/client/composer-packs.js`). Every Bot's chat shows the model that Bot runs on in its own model menu, which saves to that Bot alone: with thinking levels when the model has them, and on an agent over ACP (`acp-claude`, `acp-codex`) with the levels the agent offers for that model, or without any when it offers none. On a Bot whose plugin owns its model menu, it shows that menu. A group chat, where each member runs on its own model, and a Bot still waiting for its model show none. The plan cell and the activity and usage docks stay Omni's in every pack. Other plugins add a pack with `omni.registerComposerPack({ id, order, match(provider, target), available(env), cells: { permission, model }, hostFor })`.
- **Data**: all three keep the team's one `state.json` and its lock (automations ride it); `omni.json` is the channels plugin's, in the same folder.
- **Upgrading from one package**: a team linked to an Omni whose dsh has only this plugin shows a card in the sidebar footer that points to the plugin market for the channels plugin.

## Features

- **Long-lived Bots**: each Bot is a dsh Session in the "DS Bot" workspace, with its own name, role, instructions and model.
- **Working folders**: a Bot can work in a folder you choose instead of the team workspace, and a group chat can set one folder for all its members there. Pick it in the Bot's settings or details panel or in the group's settings, or ask a Bot (`update_bot`, `update_group`). After a change, the chat goes on in a fresh part that starts in the new folder. When a Bot sets a folder outside the team workspace, or adds a Bot to a group that works in one, it asks for your approval if those Bots can only write in their folder. Folders that hold dsh data (`$DSH_HOME`, the team's data) are refused. The team workspace itself moves in Settings > General > Locations; Bots and groups that work there go on in a fresh part in the new folder, and the old folder keeps its files.
- **Permission presets**: each Bot runs with its own dsh permission preset (Read only, Workspace or Full access), set in its details panel. A group chat can run all its members with one preset there, in place of their own: turn on **Same for every member** under Permissions in the group's settings. A new Bot starts with the team default, set under Permissions in Settings > Bots. Work a Bot opens never runs wider than the conversation that opens it. A task (`start_task`, a Genie wish) runs at the narrower of its own level and the level that conversation runs at when it starts it, such as a chat lowered with `/permission` or a read-only automation run. A Bot made with `create_bot` starts at the narrowest of its creator's level, that conversation's and its group's, and never gets a tool its creator does not have. A fresh Session a Bot's scheduled task opens starts no wider than that Bot. While a task you scheduled yourself also opens fresh Sessions, DeepSeek Harness does not say which task a fresh Session is for, so those keep the level they start with. A level that cannot be read or compared gives the narrowest one offered. What you start yourself is as before. While DSH's experimental Auto review plugin is on, **Auto review** is a preset too, marked Experimental and confirmed once when picked. Where Auto cannot hold (the plugin is off, or DSH refuses it), the Bot or group runs as Workspace and says so; a chat whose Session was left on Auto opens again once Auto review is back on. When DSH stops offering a saved level (an upgrade renames or drops it), the level stays saved and is not rewritten: a conversation that already runs is lowered to the narrowest level DSH still offers when that is known to allow less than what it has, and is otherwise left as it is; nothing new starts (a task, a greeting, a first turn in a group) until a level is picked or DSH offers the saved one again. Details and Settings → Feedback say which of these happened. Only you set permissions; Bots cannot change them.

  Auto works as Workspace on every supported route. Codex uses its own reviewer and Claude Code uses its `auto` mode. API Bots use their own model in a separate request for sandbox escalations; a granted step can leave the sandbox. Hermes, Antigravity and omp use the team's background model and are offered Auto only while one is available. Their own tools run outside DSH's sandbox.
  For bridged Codex and Claude Code, the team's background model decides DSH tool calls. If the CLI asks for permission, the rest of that prompt's bridge calls reach the person. Without a background model, bridge calls reach the person. Hard-to-undo steps and the rest of a turn after three consecutive refusals or ten total refusals always reach the person when Automagik judges. Plugin, folder and website approvals remain with the person. A request the judge decides never shows as a card, on the computer or on Pocket; only one it passes on does. A model failure asks; it never allows. Only the person turns Auto on. API marks bind the exact model; native agent marks bind their route. Bots outside Auto keep their existing behavior.

  **Auto** is Workspace plus a saved mark, chosen only by you after a confirmation in Details,
  the composer menu or the chat's permission card; the question names who decides for that Bot.
  Every message reaching the Bot's current chat counts, including another Bot's or a schedule's.
  Auto needs Workspace in the Session and this host holding the team;
  otherwise the saved choice says **Runs as Workspace here**. Picking any level, Workspace again
  included, ends Auto and its agent sessions; route and model changes clear it too.
  Deny lists coexist with Auto: changing one keeps the mark, moves the permission revision
  and ends agent sessions and outstanding grants. DSH refuses native/API and bridged denied
  calls whatever the judge says. Unbridged CLI built-ins and team agents’ own tools were
  never covered at Workspace either; they need to use DSH’s bridge for the deny to reach them.
  Tasks and Bots opened from that chat while Auto counts there inherit it; an inherited task
  counts only while the opener's mark and permission revision match. Groups, Settings and the
  team default offer no Auto row.
- **Permission stops**: a stopped step shows in the sidebar and Live rail, beside its tool call or in its group round, and on a working task card. Stops outside the visible conversation get a system notification where notifications are already allowed; a child or late group stop also notifies when that conversation cannot draw it. Pocket shows an English hint at the end of an own-chat turn. Stops live in memory and are lost on restart. The first stop per reason and turn also adds one diagnostics line in Settings → Feedback. A refusal nobody answered tells the Bot so, Auto review's final denial gives its reason, a subagent's unasked refusals reach its parent, and a coding CLI's held turn answers in the interface language.
- **Subagents**: in-process children of Read only, Workspace and Auto review Bots keep that level with approval prompts on, without changing their captured sandbox. Their asks appear above the composer of the Bot's chat or task (open it from the task card), or in the group member card; the sidebar, Live rail and notifications also show that they wait. Children keep DSH's refusal, shown as a permission stop, when their Bot runs at Full access, with approval prompts off, or at a custom or unknown level; when the Bot's level changed while the child was being created; when a resumed child has its prompts off; and when they belong to an automation run, a plugin Session, an earlier part or an ended task. An ask nothing here can answer is cancelled and noted as a stop. The phone does not show child asks.
- **Hard steps and repeated refusals**: at Read only, Workspace and DSH Auto review,
  recursive deletes, force pushes, remote branch deletes, hard resets and cleans,
  infrastructure destroys, database drops, file-tool deletes and deleting a Bot or group,
  secret files/token commands, external messages, shared or ambiguous pushes, and deletes
  outside the Bot’s folder ask the person when the existing tool gate allows them. Children follow the same check.
  Read-only team lookups such as `recall` do not ask just because their arguments mention a hard step.
  Auto also asks about these steps inside its Workspace boundary; its judge keeps its own counts.
  Plugins classify external senders through `rt.stepHooks.sendsOutside(fn)`; a failed hook asks.
  Ordinary example env files, public SSH keys, feature-branch pushes with an explicit
  destination and local file deletes stay out of the added list; a bare `git push` or a
  destination of `HEAD` asks. Exact boundaries are in RFC 0031’s #1092 amendment.
  The judge’s deadline covers model lookup too; grants bind arguments. `rt.autoAuditRows()`
  exposes its last 200 decisions without arguments, including allows, outside the failures list.
  After three consecutive automatic refusals or ten in a turn, the next refusal asks
  “Let it keep working?” Allow once only lets work continue: nothing refused runs.
  Reject stops the Bot for that turn. If approvals are off or no chat, group seat or working
  task can show the question, work stops with a reason and an automatic-stop notification
  when that host hook is available. Full access is unchanged.
  Unbridged Claude Code gets session-only ask rules for expressible hard steps at every
  asking level, removed by restarting its session across Full access. Bridged Claude has no
  Bash of its own: its DSH calls use the checks above. Codex's own tools are excluded:
  prompt rules under its Full access `never` policy refuse instead of asking, rules have no
  per-session path, and its `agent` mode sends prompt rules to its reviewer, not the person.
  This is an unmet dependency: Codex built-ins run without `session/request_permission`.
  Enforcing the list needs a mandatory per-session ask policy before its reviewer or a blocking
  pre-execution request with tool, arguments and cwd. Claude wildcard rules cannot express
  outside-folder deletes or ambiguous push targets either; those need a bridge or richer policy.

- **Bots work together**: `message_bot` sends a message to another Bot, `create_bot`, `update_bot` and `delete_bot` add, set up and remove Bots (including a profile photo from a local image file or a data URL), and `ask_user` asks you a question without blocking the other Bots. `show_view` draws a card in a Bot's own chat — text, metrics, tables, progress, choices, confirmations and short forms; an interactive card waits for your answer.
- **Group chats**: members speak one at a time, and each one reads the latest messages first. A message can `@Name` a member to pass the turn on; type `@` to pick one from a list. **+ → Reference a chat** adds another Bot's chat to a message as context, and in a group the members who answer get it. A member with nothing new to add stays quiet (`[PASS]`). Each member has its own hidden Session per group, so a group never reads a Bot's private chat.
- **Roles and permissions**:

  | Who | Can do |
  |---|---|
  | You | Everything |
  | Main Bot (there can be more than one) | Manage every group; change and delete Bots |
  | Group admin | Manage its own group only (name, notice, members, reply mode) |
  | Member | Speak in the group, `@` another member, and post into its groups from outside them |

- **Scheduled tasks and restricted Bots**: a Bot with a deny list cannot create or
  edit a scheduled task, because a `new` or `new_once` target opens a Session no deny
  layer binds; the tasks it already armed are paused and their record stays. A
  delivery no team lineage can bind is refused while such a task cannot be paused;
  when the pause lands, dsh is asked to drive again and the refused delivery goes
  through. A reminder due during the boot window, before the team has loaded, is
  refused the same way and lands once the team loads.
- **Long chats stay inside the model's window**: dsh's own compaction never runs on a Bot's Session. When a turn ends past the check line (a share of the model's context window), a small separate model call, the context steward, reads the latest messages of the chat and decides once. If the work is still under way, the chat is condensed in place into a checkpoint: a handoff summary plus your recent messages word for word. If the work has reached a stopping point, the Bot writes a handoff note and continues in a new part. Either way you still see one chat, with no marker. Earlier parts and condensed messages stay searchable in a full-text index (`node:sqlite` FTS5) through `read_own_chat`. These side calls (steward, note, checkpoint) never go to an agent over ACP (Claude Code, Codex): they run on the team's background model, and a Bot with no model that answers beside its agent skips them, says so once in the log, and past the hard line continues in a new part that carries its latest messages word for word, without a model call. Switching a Bot from an agent to an API model measures the chat against that model's own switch threshold (computed as DSH's compaction does) before DSH checks it: below it nothing happens; above it, the chat is condensed into a checkpoint only when you picked a background model in Settings and the chat fits that model (it is the one charged), and otherwise the Bot continues in a new part with the latest messages that fit, no note and no model call. The part it leaves is archived only once the new part's first answer comes from the chosen model; if that first call fails, the Bot goes back to the part it left. No message is deleted either way.
- **Memory**: each Bot keeps notes across all its conversations, each group chat keeps its own for its members, and the team shares one more. See [Memory](#memory).
- **Web search**: see [Web search](#web-search).
- **Bot browser**: each Bot drives a browser of its own: it opens pages, clicks, types, uploads and downloads. Posting, uploading, downloading and deleting ask you first, and payments always come back to you. See [Bot browser](#bot-browser).
- **Side chat**: ask a Bot about its work while it runs, in the side panel (`/side`, or `/btw` as before), without stopping its turn or adding to its chat. Nothing runs to answer.
- **Images**: for a model that cannot read images, a vision model first turns the image into text.
- **Secrets**: a Bot asks for an API key or token with a card in its own chat and never sees the value. See [Secrets](#secrets).
- **Usage**: Settings → Usage shows token usage by time (24 hours to 12 months, or days picked on a calendar), by Bot and by model, with a page for each Bot and each model. Calls that a Session logs are read from the logs, so older chats count too. Calls that leave no log (checkpoints, handoff notes, the steward, image readings, dsh titles and compaction) are counted while they stream, from the time the plugin runs. Legacy aggregates can omit provider fields; they do not claim a cross-provider cache percentage. Tokens only, no cost.
- **Official right sidebar**: every Bot chat can open Live as a tab in DSH's own pane, rather than a second fixed rail. DSH owns its collapse, focus, docking and narrow-screen behavior. Existing Browser, side-chat and plugin routes remain available.
- **Advanced Bot**: Bot Settings has a per-Bot switch, initially off and saved across parts and restarts. It reveals supported native session controls, Context and Stats without changing identity, permissions, model access or context policy. Models and permissions remain managed by the canonical Bot controls. Ordinary DSH keeps its native conversation surface.
- **Advanced Context**: shows current part/checkpoint boundaries, measured or estimated usage and effective usable/check/hard windows. Per-Bot check threshold and recent-message carry budget override host defaults (80% and 16,384 tokens); the 95% hard safety threshold is protected and effective carry is additionally capped by the check line. **Checkpoint now** requires an idle, loaded own-chat Session and condenses that same Session through Bot maintenance; stale, running, cancelled or read-only requests fail rather than bypass the native guard. **Start new part** is separate, confirmed and carries nothing from the old part. Native manual Bot compaction remains unavailable, with an explanation. Automatic memory review has separate own-chat controls/status and no guaranteed ordering with compaction; a host-wide off setting cannot be overridden.
- **Advanced Stats**: read-only last-request, last-turn, current-Session and Bot-total scopes show input/output/cache read/cache write, logical calls, recorded attempts and retries where reported. Session drilldown is limited to that Bot's own-chat parts; Bot totals partition group, task/child and tagged memory/steward/checkpoint/handoff overhead without adding overlapping scopes together. Unlinked overhead is not guessed into a request or turn. Missing is **Unknown**, not zero; legacy provenance cannot be reconstructed. Cache ratios are token-weighted within compatible, explicitly identified provider normalization, with their prompt-token denominator displayed; providers are never averaged together. Refresh may update the derived ledger but never runs a model or changes a Session. Partial history is labeled. No cost, timing, task-success or native-DSH effectiveness comparison is inferred.
- **DSH bots**: New… → New DSH bot creates a native DSH identity with a name, project folder and preset, and immediately adds team membership: the native DSH conversation UI and tooling stay available alongside roster, messages, groups and browser access. It has the same final shape as adopting an existing DSH bot, with one sidebar row and a retained original registration. Membership failure fails creation and cleans up the new registration and Session. If archival or required persistence is unavailable, a durable pending-creation registration retains ownership and tool restrictions, stays hidden from both rosters, and retries cleanup on the next load (including restart). The error reports pending cleanup; it never reports successful standalone creation. Cleanup waits for an operation-bound terminal receipt in `agent-creations/<UUID>.json`, published atomically by the allocation's producer only after native creation settles—even if that producer lost the team lock or was disposed. This receipt contains only operation and Session IDs plus outcome, grants no team-write or archival authority, and is removed after durable membership or cleanup. Missing/invalid receipts (including a hard kill before publication or receipt persistence failure) retain hidden pending ownership rather than guessing that an absent Session cannot appear later; back up `agent-creations/` with the team file while creation is pending. Cleanup is claimed durably before archival so an old producer cannot re-adopt an archived Session. DSH archival and the team file are not atomic: a failed post-archive save can temporarily retain a pending reference to an archived Session, which idempotent retry removes. For compatibility, legacy `add-agent` callers without `teamMember: true` and `rt.dshBots` keep the standalone DSH registration/session contract (no team tools); the UI explicitly opts into membership. A Bot's one-off work (`start_task`) runs under that Bot and reports back when its first turn ends.
- **Adopting a DSH bot**: **Adopt as Bot** adds team membership without replacing the DSH identity, native conversation surface, preset, avatar or capabilities. The newest Session becomes its team chat and earlier Sessions remain readable parts; nothing is renamed or recreated. `list_bots`, messages, groups, capabilities and tasks become available. Fresh parts, group member Sessions and tasks inherit its preset. The original DSH registration stays saved with an `adoptedBotId` reference, but is hidden from the standalone roster to avoid duplicate rows.
  - **Rollback**: the local `POST /api/omni-ui` endpoint `agent-bot-rollback`, payload `{ "agentId": "<original DSH id>" }`, removes only the added membership and restores the original registration and team-tool restrictions. It does not archive Sessions. Remove Main Bot/group roles first; rollback refuses new parts or tasks rather than discarding new team history. Ordinary Bot deletion refuses adopted registrations; roll back first. A failed adoption/rollback save restores the pre-operation records. This cannot reconstruct identities already removed by the older destructive implementation: those require the original registration from a backup and verified preset/avatar information; no identity is inferred from a Bot's name.
- **Make it yours**: name, role, instructions, model and look (20 characters and 12 colors, or a photo from the ones you added) for each Bot. An adopted DSH identity wears DSH's blue whale until it has a look of its own; ordinary Bots retain their identity-derived defaults and a Genie keeps its genie-clay pet; a theme, an accent color and an avatar animation level (quiet, normal or lively) for the team. A pinned Bot or group chat shows a small pushpin in the sidebar. Settings has these pages: General (look), Bots (Main Bots and each Bot's settings), Group chats (each group's settings), Connectors, Capabilities, Scheduled tasks, Usage, Secrets, Feedback and About DS Bot (versions, updates and links).

## Install

The [project page](../../README.md#install) has the full steps for dsh Desktop and dsh Web. In short:

- dsh Desktop: Settings → Plugins → add a `.tgz` of this package (`npm pack` in this folder).
- Command line: `dsh plugin --profile web add /path/to/automagik-bots-dsh-<version>.tgz`.
- Or skip dsh setup entirely: the Automagik desktop app ([`apps/desktop`](../desktop/README.md), `omni desktop` from Omni's CLI) ships dsh with this plugin on a home of its own.

To work on the plugins from a checkout, add them to a dsh profile as linked dependencies and bundles (the channels and canvas plugins are optional):

```json
{
  "dependencies": {
    "@automagik/bots-dsh": "link:/path/to/apps/bots-dsh",
    "@automagik/omni-channels-dsh": "link:/path/to/omni/apps/omni-channels-dsh",
    "@automagik/omni-canvas-dsh": "link:/path/to/omni/apps/omni-canvas-dsh"
  },
  "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["@deepseek-ai/dsh-base", "@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app", "@automagik/bots-dsh", "@automagik/omni-channels-dsh", "@automagik/omni-canvas-dsh"] } }
}
```

Run `pnpm install` in the profile folder, then start dsh from the deepseek-harness repository:

```sh
pnpm -s dsh --profile web --no-open
```

The first time the team opens, the plugin creates a Main Bot called Omni.

**Upgrading from the `ds-bot` builds of the Omni UI**: earlier builds were named `ds-bot` with the plugin id `bot` and kept the team in `~/.dsh/bot`. Replace `ds-bot` with `@automagik/bots-dsh` in the profile, and set `importHome: ~/.dsh/bot` once (see [Configuration](#configuration)) to copy that team into `~/.omni/ui`; the old folder is left as it was. Browser settings saved under `ds-bot:` are not carried over, because DS Bot uses the same names.

## Connect to an Omni

This needs the Omni channels plugin. On the Channels page, type the address of an Omni (for example `omni.example.com`) and choose **Get a code**. Omni answers with a short code and the WhatsApp number of its pairing channel; send the code to yourself from that WhatsApp ("Message yourself"; **Open WhatsApp** or the QR opens the chat with the code typed). The page goes live as soon as the code arrives. The Omni must have pairing turned on (`OMNI_PAIRING_ENABLED=true` and a pairing instance on the server).
