# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.0.9-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-206-brightgreen) ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-ai-terminal-pet?label=dsh%20plugin)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Demo](docs/assets/demo.gif)
*The actual sequence: a session blocks on a permission prompt and the strip breathes, hovering unfolds the session list, and clicking the arrow at the end of the waiting row brings that terminal forward. Frames are rasterized from the shipped renderer; the ring stands in for the click, since a layered window draws no cursor.*

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

![In context](docs/assets/desktop-scene.png)
*In context: the strip sits at the screen edge beside two terminals, so a blocked session is visible without switching windows. The panel is the real renderer output; the two terminals around it are drawn, since a real capture would contain somebody's project names.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Copy a project path | Click a session row (or the copy half of the compact strip) to put that conversation's working directory on the clipboard; a short pill over the row confirms it, and a failed copy says so instead of claiming success. Rows whose reporter sent no working directory keep their old meaning: clicking them collapses the panel. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Clicking anywhere that is not a session row or a control toggles compact and expanded; drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor; the wheel zooms between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native four-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions, Look) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts when a session starts waiting for you, fails, or finishes — one pure policy decides (see below), so a prompt you are already reading does not also pop a balloon. |
| Attentiveness | An alert depends on what the session is asking for and whether you are looking: approval / question / plan review are told apart from the reason reporters already send, keyboard-and-mouse idle time is read from the OS, and the window that owns the session is resolved with the same ranking jump-to-terminal uses. Unmeasurable facts alert rather than stay quiet. |
| Per-session mute and unread | Right-click a session row to mute or unmute that conversation; a suppressed alert still marks its row unread, cleared by jumping to it, by it running again, or by it disappearing. Muting never silences the auto-approve countdown, which is a safety control, not a notification. |
| Alert receipt | The last alert decision is written to `alerts.json` beside `config.json` - not in `runtime/`, where every `*.json` is a reporter snapshot and the scanner deletes what it cannot parse - and printed by `--json` under `alerts` and summarised by the tenth `--doctor` check, so "why was I not told" has an answer instead of folklore. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

There are three ways in. Pick the one that matches how you got here.

**A. DeepSeek Harness user — no Go toolchain, nothing to build**

```powershell
dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet
```

The package carries a prebuilt overlay and this project's own `protocol.js`. On first load it copies them into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` **only when they are missing**, so it never overwrites an install you maintain yourself. That is the whole setup: the panel appears on the next session. It is also on npm as [`dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-ai-terminal-pet) (1.2.18), and the release tarball, a tag-pinned git source and a bare repository URL all work (`dsh plugin add <path-or-git-url>`); the same bootstrap runs either way. It targets DeepSeek Harness 0.2.x (`engines.dsh` `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0`, Node 24.9+); a 0.1.x host is not covered, and such a host refuses the bundle instead of loading it untested.

**B. Everyone else — download a package, no Go toolchain**

Two packages are published for this release: a self-extracting `pet-setup.exe` and a portable zip. Both install the same 11 artifacts into the same directory; the zip additionally lets you look inside before running anything.

1. Download one of them from the [`pet-v1.0.7` release](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/tag/pet-v1.0.9):
   - **`pet-setup.exe`** (14,309,888 B, 13.65 MiB): double-click it. It verifies its own payload against `SHA256SUMS.txt` **before** writing anything, then runs the installer inside itself. `pet-setup.exe --verify` re-checks the installed files at any time, `--uninstall` removes them, `--add-to-path` puts the commands on your PATH.
   - **`ai-terminal-pet-1.0.9-win-x64.zip`** (5,054,473 B, 17 files): unzip it anywhere and double-click `install.cmd`. Everything is inspectable first; `install.cmd -VerifyOnly`, `-Uninstall` and `-AddToPath` work as they do in the source tree.
2. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```

The zip and the setup exe carry the three binaries, `protocol.js`, the Harness bundle, the installer and a `SHA256SUMS.txt`, so the only thing on Windows is one download and one double-click. Neither needs Go, Node, or an installer framework. The release is **not code-signed yet**, so the first run shows SmartScreen's "unknown publisher" prompt:

![SmartScreen on an unsigned build](docs/assets/smartscreen-unsigned.png)
*What an unsigned build produces on a machine that has never seen it: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. This image is a reconstruction of the documented dialog, not a capture - see [docs/assets/README.md](docs/assets/README.md).*

That prompt is a certificate the project does not have, not a problem with the file you downloaded — the per-file SHA256 values in `SHA256SUMS.txt` are the honest substitute until a certificate exists.

After installing, `--doctor` should look like this (paths shortened here, everything else is the program's own output):

![--doctor on a healthy install](docs/assets/doctor-green.png)
*Ten checks, and the one that matters when you see an empty panel is `instance` — if it says a live instance is listening, the overlay is healthy and the missing piece is the terminal's reporter, not the install.*

**C. Developers — build from source (Go 1.23+)**

```powershell
# 1. Build the overlay, the native statusline shim and the native hook
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-hook.exe ./cmd/pet-hook

# 2. Install (stops a running overlay, copies, re-hashes every artifact)
.\scripts\install.cmd

# 3. See it work
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
```

Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -VerifyOnly
```

It prints `install: verified - 11 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 11 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, the native hook `pet-hook.exe`, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle). The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.

`install.cmd` is the entry point rather than `install.ps1` because a stock Windows install runs PowerShell at `RemoteSigned`, and `RemoteSigned` refuses a local `.ps1` that still carries the "downloaded from the internet" zone marker — the exact shape of a file you unzip from a release. The wrapper starts one `powershell.exe` with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, changes no machine or user policy, forwards every argument and every exit code, and adds no install logic: `install.ps1` remains the only implementation, and `.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` works unchanged on a machine whose policy already allows it.

Put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -AddToPath
```

It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.cmd -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugins` in `opencode.json` (OpenCode 2.x: the file is a plugin with an `id` and a `setup`) | Turn, tool and permission states, including the difference between "waiting for you" and "still working" |
| Claude Code | Add `& "%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\pet-hook.exe" --mode=claude` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json`. `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` still works and is the fallback when you cannot run the `.exe`. | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `pet-hook.exe --mode=antigravity` for agent and tool events (`antigravity-hook.js` is the fallback) | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. The package is now **1.2.18** (tag `dsh-plugin-v1.2.18`, asset `dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.18.tgz`); 1.2.15 and everything before it stay published and immutable but are superseded. 1.2.15 was the DSH 0.2.x compatibility release: `engines.dsh` moved to `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0` and `engines.node` to `>=24.9.0`, after installing the tarball into a real 0.2.0-rc.1 host and a real 0.2.2-rc.3 host. 1.2.16 changes no code either: the package now ships a Chinese README next to the English one (`README.zh.md`, which is what turns a catalogue's "only an English version exists" note into a real Chinese page) and its `dsh.catalog` summary leads with the question the overlay answers. 1.2.9 through 1.2.16 carry overlay 1.0.3 through 1.0.7 (1.2.12 and 1.2.13 both carry 1.0.6; 1.2.14, 1.2.15 and 1.2.16 all carry 1.0.7): 1.0.3 turned alerts into a decision with a written receipt (`alerts.json`, which `--json` and `--doctor` read back); 1.0.4 moved that receipt next to `config.json`, because the runtime scanner deletes any snapshot file in `runtime/` it cannot parse; 1.0.5 made a click on a session row copy its project path and answer with an on-panel receipt; 1.0.6 tracked down three phantom alerts (a vanished session no longer counts as a completion, one conversation is one row, and OpenCode 2.x events map to the states they mean); 1.0.7 rebuilt the settings window - four real type sizes instead of two, hints that wrap instead of being cut with an ellipsis, its own DPI, and a Look tab that finally switches. 1.2.7 shipped the 1.0.1 overlay, whose compact strip answers "which terminal is blocked, and for how long" without expanding the panel; 1.2.8 shipped 1.0.2, where the look itself became a setting - three named palettes, an optional per-terminal tint on each row's source name, and "start hidden". 1.2.5 is the first version that works on a machine that never ran the overlay: it declares `vendor/package.json` as CommonJS (without it, `require()` of the shipped protocol returned a namespace with no `sendStatus`, so a `DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1` install silently reported nothing), it reads the project path, lineage and start time from the session header instead of `process.cwd()` (the desktop Harness starts from the install directory, so every session was attributed to one wrong path), and its de-duplication signature now covers state, reason, tool, project, title and parent session instead of state alone. 1.2.4 was a wording fix (one market install read as if it covered every terminal, and it does not - the bundle mirrors **Harness** sessions out of the box, while OpenCode, Claude Code and Antigravity sessions appear only after each of those terminals gets its own reporter); 1.2.3 added the `dsh.marketplace` block a third-party storefront reads before offering a plugin to its desktop client, and 1.2.2 moved the installer from the repository root into `scripts/`, which edits Go comments, which changes the source digest `vendor/manifest.json` records. Release assets cannot be edited, so a wording or manifest fix costs a version - shipping different bytes under an unchanged version is exactly the drift this repository removes. The three install forms are verified end to end, and the 1.2.4 assets were installed again from three fresh directories after the release went out: the release tarball in **1.8 s**, the tag-pinned git source in **3.7 s**, and the repository URL in **6.5 s**, all rc=0, with the unpacked bytes matching `git show ff7f6de:` file for file (a bare `add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` still waits on the npm release described below):

```powershell
# from the release tarball: no git clone, no build step
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.18/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.18.tgz

# from git, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.18&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"

# from the repository URL: resolves through the root manifest shim
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add github:jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet
```

The repository URL works because the repository root now carries a 68-line `package.json` shim that contains no code: it points `main` at the package, declares `dsh.bundle.patch` as `./packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet/cordis.patch.yml` and limits `files` to that subtree. Without it a host that reads the repository root sees no `dsh.bundle`, installs an empty package and warns `declares no dsh.bundle`. The shim is `private`, so it never occupies the npm name, its `version` tracks the package (`verify.mjs` asserts they are equal, so a bump cannot land in one manifest only), and it carries the same `dsh.catalog` block the package does.

The package ships no lifecycle hooks at all — `prepack` was removed in 1.1.0 — because pnpm runs them for a git dependency and fails an unpinned source with an `allowBuilds` error that never mentions AI Terminal Pet. `vendor/` is committed instead and only verified: `node scripts/vendor.mjs --check` re-hashes the two vendored files and checks `vendor/manifest.json` against them, writing nothing. One form still fails, for a different reason: `git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet` without a `#ref` — pnpm concatenates the fragments and asks `ls-remote` for a repository that does not exist, so it reports `repository ... not found`.

1.2.0 also makes the package self-describing: `dsh.catalog` declares a `category` (`tool`), a one-line summary in English and Chinese, and five `capabilities` — `windows-overlay`, `named-pipe`, `session-state`, `tray-icon`, `no-network`. Those capabilities are **self-declared and unenforced**; dsh does not sandbox plugins, so the block describes what the overlay already does rather than granting it permission to do so. `keywords` gained `dsh-plugin`, the tag auto-indexing marketplaces harvest. 1.2.3 adds `dsh.marketplace` next to `dsh.bundle` and `dsh.catalog`: `profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`, `requiresBuildApproval: false` and `manualSteps: false`. That field is read by third-party registries, not by DSH - the plugin mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way, and this bundle only subscribes to `session/event`, so no profile-specific service is involved: that makes two independent discovery paths — registry review (a reviewed entry merges into `main` and only then appears in the list) and topic/keyword harvesting (no application needed at all). Two marketplaces already harvest automatically: [LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop](https://github.com/LivXue/dsh-plugin-shop) rebuilds daily from npm metadata, and every entry in its published shard is pinned by tarball integrity, so a Git-only package cannot appear there until it reaches npm; [zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store](https://github.com/zasenjc/dsh-plugins-store) syncs every 30 minutes and lists any public repository carrying both the `dsh-plugin` and `deepseek-harness` topics.

Its payload carries a prebuilt overlay and this project's own `protocol.js`, copied into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` on first use **only when they are missing** — an existing install is never overwritten, and the overlay keeps running entirely on its own, so a machine that only wants the pet still needs nothing but `scripts/install.cmd`. Its entry in the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) registry ([PR #13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937)) passed both upstream checks and was merged on 2026-11-10, so the upstream catalogue lists the entry (that file pins which tarball the entry installs and can only be changed by pull request against that repository, never by an edit here: [PR #14076](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/14076) moved it to 1.2.2 and merged at 19:59:37Z, and [PR #14089](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/14089) moved it to 1.2.3 and merged at 2026-11-10T21:10:15Z, so the next rebuild renders that asset while [PR #14243](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/14243), opened on 2026-11-11, carries 1.2.4 and adds the same "other terminals need their own reporter" sentence to both descriptions; [imsai-sh/awesome-deepseek-harness-plugins PR #912](https://github.com/imsai-sh/awesome-deepseek-harness-plugins/pull/912) makes the same wording fix there, and that repository never auto-merges an edit to an existing entry, so it waits for a maintainer; #14063, which had targeted 1.2.1, was closed once 1.2.2 packed the corrected bytes); the rendered catalogue page returned 404 at 16:16Z and became reachable later the same day once the upstream site build finished (`42844452013`, started 15:27:09Z, concluded 16:39:27Z); the catalogue file that DSH's in-app Market actually loads (`plugins.json`; its `count` was 10119 before that build and 10,304 when re-read after the 1.2.3 release) contains this repository too, but its `install` command is rendered from that `tarball` field at build time, so the copy read after the merge still emitted the 1.2.0 asset; the next rebuild rendered 1.2.2, then #14089 carried 1.2.3 past that when it merged at 2026-11-10T21:10:15Z. In a comment on the pull request the maintainer explained that he trimmed the merged description himself: for a Harness session the panel only mirrors state and jumps to the DSH window, so approving still happens inside DSH. The [DSH-Plugins-Marketplace](https://github.com/bradeGithub/DSH-Plugins-Marketplace) index picked this repository up automatically; its 18:08:44Z rebuild on 2026-11-10 records `pkg_name`/`version`, the verdict `bundle-plugin`, and now `risk_tier: "safe"` with an empty `risk_flags` list. That is not a favour granted by an allowlist: the scanner only fetches root-level `install.ps1`/`install.sh`/`package.json` and regex-scans them, and the two lines it used to match (`CurrentVersion\Run` and `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force`) moved into `scripts/` together with the installer, so those rules have no input left (the behaviour itself is unchanged). The DSH in-app Discover index accepts an npm version or a git source pinned to a 40-character commit. # dsh-ai-terminal-pet

**English** · [中文](./README.zh.md)

A DeepSeek Harness (DSH) Cordis bundle that mirrors Harness session state onto
the [AI Terminal Pet](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet) desktop
overlay: a small always-on-top Win32 pet that shows which sessions are working,
which one is waiting for your approval, which failed, and which finished.

The package ships the overlay binary and the official reporter protocol module
inside the tarball, so a single market install is enough to get a pet on screen
that follows **this Harness's** sessions. It does not attach to any other
terminal by itself: sessions from OpenCode, Claude Code and Antigravity appear
only after that terminal's own reporter is installed into it. The repository
README section [Connect your terminal](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet#connect-your-terminal)
has one hook per terminal; the panel, the pipe and the protocol are shared, so
once a terminal reports it shows up next to the Harness sessions.

No npm dependencies, no install scripts, no network calls at runtime (unless the
maintainer pins a release in lib/release-pins.json, see below).

## What it does

| Harness signal | Overlay state |
| --- | --- |
| `turn/start`, `agent/inbox/claimed`, `agent/status` running | working |
| `tool/call` | tool_use |
| `approval/request` (waterfall listener) | waiting_permission |
| `tool/result` with `error`, `agent/error` | error |
| `turn/end`, `agent/status` idle | idle |
| Harness process exit | closed |

Events this table does not list are not part of the Harness session log: there is
no `command/done` or `working-directory/change` in `SessionEventMap`. The project
path, the parent session and the session start time do not come from events at
all - they are read from `session.header` (`cwd`, `parentSession`, `createdAt`),
which is the only place the host states them. That is also why a session shows
the right project even though the desktop Harness itself runs from its install
directory, and why a subagent conversation is nested under the session it was
forked from.

The overlay then plays an alert tone, shows a tray balloon on those transitions
and its one-click jump button targets the Harness window. Plugin reload (HMR)
disposes the listeners but deliberately does not close sessions: only a real
process exit means the conversation is over.

Panel gestures (overlay 1.0.5 and later): clicking a session row - or the left
half of the compact strip - copies that conversation's working directory to the
clipboard and shows a short "Copied" receipt over the row; clicking anywhere
else still collapses the panel. The copy is the path, not the label the row
prints.

![Copy receipt](../../docs/assets/overlay-copy.png)
*The receipt after a click on a session row: the path is on the clipboard and the
row says so for about a second. A failed copy says "Copy failed" instead of
claiming success.*

## Where it is listed, and what each market indexes

Three independent paths exist today, and each one reads a different field:

| Market | What it indexes | What this package offers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| npm registry | package name, version, `dist.integrity` | published as `dsh-ai-terminal-pet`; a market that installs by name gets a verified tarball |
| dshmarket (the market tab most Harness Desktop users run) | `https://awesome-dsh-plugin.com/plugins.json`, which is generated from the [awesome-dsh-plugin](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin) repository | entry merged via PR [#13937](https://github.com/awesome-dsh-plugin/awesome-dsh-plugin/pull/13937); the `install` command it renders comes from that entry's pinned `tarball`, so bumping it is always a pull request *there*, never an edit here |
| GitHub-harvesting markets | repositories carrying the `dsh-plugin` topic plus a root `package.json` declaring `name` and `dsh.bundle` | this repository has the topic and the root shim manifest, which is what makes `dsh plugin add github:owner/repo` resolve instead of mounting a 0.0.0 dependency |

"Listed" and "visible" are different states, and only the second one helps a
user: the awesome entry existed before its `plugins.json` entry did, because the
site builds the catalog on a schedule. Check the market's own public index, not
the merged pull request. The package README cannot promise what another
repository's build will render; it can only promise that the fields those builds
read are present and correct.

The package describes itself to storefronts through `dsh.catalog`: a category, a
one-line summary in both languages, and the capabilities it uses. Capabilities
are self-declared and never checked — DSH does not sandbox plugins — so read them
as a description, not a permission grant.
The bundle is Windows only and declares `dsh.bundle.platforms: ["win32"]`, so
other platforms show it as unsupported instead of installing it.

It also declares `dsh.marketplace` (`profiles: ["desktop", "headless", "web"]`,
`requiresBuildApproval: false`, `manualSteps: false`). DSH itself never reads
that field - the bundle mounts through `dsh.bundle` either way - but storefronts
that sort entries by profile do: without it a registry falls back to a
headless-or-web guess and a desktop client hides the entry.

Manually, from a terminal, into a profile you own — by package name, by release
tarball, or by pinning the release tag. All three are verified end to end:

```sh
# by package name: published on npm, no clone, no Go toolchain
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add dsh-ai-terminal-pet

# release tarball: same bytes as the npm release, straight from the GitHub Release
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/download/dsh-plugin-v1.2.18/dsh-ai-terminal-pet-1.2.18.tgz

# git source, pinned to the release tag
dsh plugin --profile <profile> add "git+https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet.git#dsh-plugin-v1.2.18&path:/packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet"
```

Those three differ only in transport. The npm path is the shortest and the one a
market uses when it installs by name; the tarball path works when a market pins a
release asset instead of a registry entry; the git path is the fallback for a
machine that cannot reach npm at all. Every one of them lands the same
prebuilt overlay in `vendor/`.

Do not hand pnpm a bare repository URL. pnpm resolves a git dependency by
running the package's lifecycle scripts, and it blocks those for unpinned
git sources until you copy the `allowBuilds` key it prints into your profile's
`pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the failure message never mentions AI Terminal Pet. The
package therefore ships no lifecycle hook, and its vendored overlay is a
committed file rather than a build product. `vendor/manifest.json` records the
SHA-256 of that file, the SHA-256 of the Go sources it was built from, and the
Go version that produced it, so a stale or hand-edited vendor directory fails a
check instead of shipping quietly.

The GitHub and npm paths above need nothing from this repository at install time.
`dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet` resolves through the npm registry; the
tarball and git forms resolve through GitHub. A marketplace that indexes npm
sees the package under its own name and can verify the published integrity
digest; a marketplace that indexes repositories sees the `dsh-plugin` topic and
the root shim manifest.

`add` is the whole install: the profile records the dependency, and the bundle
declares itself through `dsh.bundle.patch`, so no separate `enable` step exists.
The profile you add it to has to be the one Harness boots.

Two profiles are special. The reserved `desktop` profile is rejected by the
standalone `dsh` CLI (`profile "desktop" is managed exclusively by the Electron
application`); the Desktop app's own bundled CLI does accept it, and the in-app
plugin manager is the supported path there. Any other profile name is yours.

If the app reports restart-required after enabling the bundle, restart Harness.

## What it writes on disk

First use in a Harness process copies two files, and only when they are missing:

| File | Origin | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js | vendor/protocol.js | pipe name, state set, redaction, snapshot |
| %LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | vendor/AI-Terminal-Pet.exe | the Win32 overlay |

Nothing is ever overwritten: an existing file, including one placed by the
standalone installer, wins. Set DSH_PET_NO_BOOTSTRAP=1 to skip this step
entirely (for example when the overlay is managed by `scripts/install.ps1` already).

Reports also write the overlay's normal runtime snapshot under the same
directory, exactly like every other reporter.

### Optional download fallback

lib/release-pins.json is absent from the published package by default. When the
maintainer fills it in with pinned release asset URLs, sizes and SHA-256
digests, a machine that has no vendored binary downloads the two assets over
HTTPS with a 30 s timeout, verifies size and digest with node:crypto, and only
then installs them. Any failure is silent apart from one warning; the plugin
keeps working without an overlay.

## The overlay itself is still standalone

This bundle is a convenience. The overlay is a Go application that installs
normally with `scripts/install.ps1` from the repository, and every other reporter
(Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, generic) talks to the same named pipe.
Those reporters are separate installs, not part of this package: a terminal that
has none of them hooked reports nothing, in this install or in any other. A
machine that only wants the overlay does not need this package; a machine that
only wants the plugin gets one installed automatically.

## Requirements and limits

- Windows only (named pipes plus a Win32 layered window).
- DeepSeek Harness 0.2.x. `engines.dsh` is `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0`, and since DSH
  0.2.1-alpha.3 the host reads that range alone: a bundle whose range the running
  DSH does not satisfy is refused and the profile rolled back, so the range is the
  whole compatibility statement. The `-0` bounds are deliberate - DSH evaluates
  the range with semver's `includePrerelease`, under which `<0.3.0` still admits
  `0.3.0-rc.1` and `>=0.2.0` still refuses `0.2.0-rc.1`. Both ends were measured
  against the host's own compatibility function. It was verified by installing
  this tarball into a real 0.2.0-rc.1 host and a real 0.2.2-rc.3 host and
  composing its layer with `dsh --dump-config`.
- Node 24.9+ in the Harness runtime, which is what DSH 0.2.x itself requires.
- Nothing in this package can fail the host: every entry point is wrapped,
  every report is fire-and-forget, and there is no process.exit.
- Session id is the Harness session.header.id; pid is a synthetic per-session
  id and parentPid is the real Harness process, which is how the overlay ties a
  session to its terminal window.

# ai-terminal-pet

Stop glancing across terminal windows to track agent states. It costs one small executable with no account and no cloud.

![ai-terminal-pet](docs/assets/hero.png)

![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-Windows-blue) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/go-1.23-00ADD8) ![Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/version-1.0.9-blue)
![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-green) ![Size](https://img.shields.io/badge/size-4.17%20MiB-blue) ![Dependencies](https://img.shields.io/badge/dependencies-3-informational) ![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-206-brightgreen) ![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/dsh-ai-terminal-pet?label=dsh%20plugin)

> 🇬🇧 [English](#english)  ·  🇨🇳 [中文](#中文)

---

## English

### The problem

You run Claude Code, OpenCode, or Antigravity in multiple terminal windows at once. A background task prompts for permission to execute a tool, but you are focused in another window and never notice the prompt.

Fourteen minutes later, you switch back only to discover that your build has been sitting idle the entire time. Glancing across multiple terminal tabs wastes focus and breaks your concentration.

ai-terminal-pet anchors a 56px strip to the screen edge. It aggregates your sessions in real time, pulses when an agent needs permission, and displays which project is waiting and for how long.

The table below contrasts the everyday workflow before and after using the overlay:

| Context | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple terminals | Four terminal windows open; you lose track of which window needs attention. | One 56px strip on the edge of the screen aggregates every active session. |
| Blocked build | You find out a build was blocked on a permission prompt fourteen minutes ago. | The overlay pulses immediately and shows which project is waiting and for how long. |
| Context switching | You click across tabs to check whether builds and tasks are still running. | A single glance reveals current states without touching your keyboard or mouse. |

### What it looks like

![Demo](docs/assets/demo.gif)
*The actual sequence: a session blocks on a permission prompt and the strip breathes, hovering unfolds the session list, and clicking the arrow at the end of the waiting row brings that terminal forward. Frames are rasterized from the shipped renderer; the ring stands in for the click, since a layered window draws no cursor.*

![Compact strip](docs/assets/overlay-compact.png)
*Compact strip: pulsing state orb with status glyph, session count, state word, and waiting project name.*

![Expanded list](docs/assets/overlay-expanded.png)
*Expanded list: active sessions showing per-row project name, state, source hook, and relative time.*

![Many sessions](docs/assets/overlay-expanded-many.png)
*Expanded list with many sessions: six session rows followed by the overflow line showing remaining sessions.*

![Auto-approve countdown](docs/assets/overlay-auto-approve.png)
*Auto-approve countdown: draining bar with "Allow (5s)" prompt allowing manual veto before automatic permission approval.*

![In context](docs/assets/desktop-scene.png)
*In context: the strip sits at the screen edge beside two terminals, so a blocked session is visible without switching windows. The panel is the real renderer output; the two terminals around it are drawn, since a real capture would contain somebody's project names.*

---

### Features

The table below outlines the core capabilities and exact runtime parameters of the application:

| Feature | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| State aggregation | Aggregates sessions across 7 states (`idle`, `thinking`, `working`, `tool_use`, `waiting_permission`, `error`, `closed`), showing the highest-priority state across all active sessions. |
| Compact and expanded panels | Compact panel occupies 56x156 logical pixels anchored to a screen edge; clicking expands to 200 px wide, displaying 1–6 rows before adding an overflow line. |
| Copy a project path | Click a session row (or the copy half of the compact strip) to put that conversation's working directory on the clipboard; a short pill over the row confirms it, and a failed copy says so instead of claiming success. Rows whose reporter sent no working directory keep their old meaning: clicking them collapses the panel. |
| Whole-panel gestures | Clicking anywhere that is not a session row or a control toggles compact and expanded; drag anywhere moves 1:1 with the cursor; the wheel zooms between 65% and 160%. |
| Edge retract | Slides mostly off-screen when docked at an edge leaving a thin sliver; hovering restores it, while waiting_permission or error states override retraction to remain visible. |
| Tray menu | Right-click tray menu toggles visibility, resets position and zoom, opens settings, switches language, toggles autostart, and configures auto-approve. |
| Settings window | Native four-tab window (General, Sound, Sessions, Look) where every change persists immediately to `config.json` without an OK button. |
| Synthesized alert tones | Generates 44.1 kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV tones in memory across four sound schemes (`chime`, `bell`, `soft`, `pulse`), with separate gates for waiting, error, and finish. |
| Per-session alerts | Fires Windows tray notification balloons and audio alerts when a session starts waiting for you, fails, or finishes — one pure policy decides (see below), so a prompt you are already reading does not also pop a balloon. |
| Attentiveness | An alert depends on what the session is asking for and whether you are looking: approval / question / plan review are told apart from the reason reporters already send, keyboard-and-mouse idle time is read from the OS, and the window that owns the session is resolved with the same ranking jump-to-terminal uses. Unmeasurable facts alert rather than stay quiet. |
| Per-session mute and unread | Right-click a session row to mute or unmute that conversation; a suppressed alert still marks its row unread, cleared by jumping to it, by it running again, or by it disappearing. Muting never silences the auto-approve countdown, which is a safety control, not a notification. |
| Alert receipt | The last alert decision is written to `alerts.json` beside `config.json` - not in `runtime/`, where every `*.json` is a reporter snapshot and the scanner deletes what it cannot parse - and printed by `--json` under `alerts` and summarised by the tenth `--doctor` check, so "why was I not told" has an answer instead of folklore. |
| Auto-approve and denylist | Provides a 5-second veto window on permission prompts where a tap denies and silence approves; blocks commands matching the dangerous-command denylist. |
| Jump to terminal | Walks session process ancestry and matches window titles to bring the waiting terminal window or tab to the foreground. |
| Scriptable CLI | Outputs structured session state via `ai-terminal-pet --json` by reading disk snapshots, avoiding blocking on GUI processes. |
| Single instance | A named mutex makes a second launch activate the running overlay instead of starting another one. |
| Connection capacity | The pipe server accepts 32 concurrent connections with a 5 s read timeout, so IPC never blocks the UI thread. |
| Idle lifecycle | A session is dropped only after a 2-minute absence grace; with no session left, the process removes itself after 10 minutes. |

### How it works

```text
Host CLI (Claude Code / OpenCode / Antigravity)
       │
       ▼ (Fire-and-forget hooks)
reporters/*.js
       │
       ▼ (JSON line over Windows named pipe: \\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>)
AI-Terminal-Pet.exe (Go 1.23, single-instance mutex)
       │
       ├─► internal/pipeserver (32 connections, 5s timeout, OK/ERR response)
       ├─► internal/store (in-memory state, TTL, disk snapshots fallback)
       └─► internal/ui (Win32 layered window, GDI topmost canvas)
```

- **Per-user named pipe**: IPC flows through `\\.\pipe\ai-terminal-pet-v1-<8hex>`, where `<8hex>` is derived from the SHA-256 hash of the user home directory. The exact same pipe-name algorithm is implemented in Go and JavaScript, locked by a cross-language golden test.

- **JSON line protocol**: Sessions transmit one JSON line per message with a 1 MiB payload cap. The server replies with an exact `OK` or `ERR` acknowledgment, and reporters retry until a deadline without treating partial reads as success.

- **On-disk snapshots**: Snapshot files under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\runtime\` provide a fallback channel and serve as the authoritative on-disk record of active sessions.

- **OS observation over heartbeats**: Session existence is decided by operating system observation of the process table and window titles rather than reporter heartbeats. A session remains active as long as its terminal window exists, and removal requires the host to be unobservable for a continuous 2-minute grace period.

- **Disks beat heartbeats**: The disk snapshot is authoritative for session existence: a session that was on disk and is gone is over, while synthetic PIDs from hooks never participate in liveness probing.

- **Connection handling**: The server accommodates 32 concurrent connections with a 5s read timeout, keeping IPC processing off the UI thread.

- **GDI rendering**: A top-down 32bpp DIB section created with CreateDIBSection is painted through a memory DC and handed to the layered window with UpdateLayeredWindow.

### Install

There are three ways in. Pick the one that matches how you got here.

**A. DeepSeek Harness user — no Go toolchain, nothing to build**

```powershell
dsh plugin add dsh-ai-terminal-pet
```

The package carries a prebuilt overlay and this project's own `protocol.js`. On first load it copies them into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\` **only when they are missing**, so it never overwrites an install you maintain yourself. That is the whole setup: the panel appears on the next session. It is also on npm as [`dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dsh-ai-terminal-pet) (1.2.18), and the release tarball, a tag-pinned git source and a bare repository URL all work (`dsh plugin add <path-or-git-url>`); the same bootstrap runs either way. It targets DeepSeek Harness 0.2.x (`engines.dsh` `>=0.2.0-0 <0.3.0-0`, Node 24.9+); a 0.1.x host is not covered, and such a host refuses the bundle instead of loading it untested.

**B. Everyone else — download a package, no Go toolchain**

Two packages are published for this release: a self-extracting `pet-setup.exe` and a portable zip. Both install the same 11 artifacts into the same directory; the zip additionally lets you look inside before running anything.

1. Download one of them from the [`pet-v1.0.7` release](https://github.com/jjjjjjjjnnjnn/ai-terminal-pet/releases/tag/pet-v1.0.9):
   - **`pet-setup.exe`** (14,309,888 B, 13.65 MiB): double-click it. It verifies its own payload against `SHA256SUMS.txt` **before** writing anything, then runs the installer inside itself. `pet-setup.exe --verify` re-checks the installed files at any time, `--uninstall` removes them, `--add-to-path` puts the commands on your PATH.
   - **`ai-terminal-pet-1.0.9-win-x64.zip`** (5,054,473 B, 17 files): unzip it anywhere and double-click `install.cmd`. Everything is inspectable first; `install.cmd -VerifyOnly`, `-Uninstall` and `-AddToPath` work as they do in the source tree.
2. Verify that the installation works:
   ```powershell
   & "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
   ```

The zip and the setup exe carry the three binaries, `protocol.js`, the Harness bundle, the installer and a `SHA256SUMS.txt`, so the only thing on Windows is one download and one double-click. Neither needs Go, Node, or an installer framework. The release is **not code-signed yet**, so the first run shows SmartScreen's "unknown publisher" prompt:

![SmartScreen on an unsigned build](docs/assets/smartscreen-unsigned.png)
*What an unsigned build produces on a machine that has never seen it: click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. This image is a reconstruction of the documented dialog, not a capture - see [docs/assets/README.md](docs/assets/README.md).*

That prompt is a certificate the project does not have, not a problem with the file you downloaded — the per-file SHA256 values in `SHA256SUMS.txt` are the honest substitute until a certificate exists.

After installing, `--doctor` should look like this (paths shortened here, everything else is the program's own output):

![--doctor on a healthy install](docs/assets/doctor-green.png)
*Ten checks, and the one that matters when you see an empty panel is `instance` — if it says a live instance is listening, the overlay is healthy and the missing piece is the terminal's reporter, not the install.*

**C. Developers — build from source (Go 1.23+)**

```powershell
# 1. Build the overlay, the native statusline shim and the native hook
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe ./cmd/ai-terminal-pet
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-statusline.exe ./cmd/pet-statusline
go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags "-s -w" -o .\bin\pet-hook.exe ./cmd/pet-hook

# 2. Install (stops a running overlay, copies, re-hashes every artifact)
.\scripts\install.cmd

# 3. See it work
& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json
```

Re-verify the installed artifacts at any time with per-file SHA256 checks:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -VerifyOnly
```

It prints `install: verified - 11 file(s) match the repository, 0 warning(s)` and exits 0 only when every deployed artifact matches (the 11 artifacts are the overlay, the statusline shim, the native hook `pet-hook.exe`, `protocol.js`, and the 7 files of the DeepSeek Harness bundle). The installer itself stops a running overlay first and waits for the process to release its file handles; a plain file copy over a live binary fails at random, which is what the retry loop and the SHA256 comparison after every copy are for.

`install.cmd` is the entry point rather than `install.ps1` because a stock Windows install runs PowerShell at `RemoteSigned`, and `RemoteSigned` refuses a local `.ps1` that still carries the "downloaded from the internet" zone marker — the exact shape of a file you unzip from a release. The wrapper starts one `powershell.exe` with `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`, changes no machine or user policy, forwards every argument and every exit code, and adds no install logic: `install.ps1` remains the only implementation, and `.\scripts\install.ps1 -VerifyOnly` works unchanged on a machine whose policy already allows it.

Put `ai-terminal-pet` on your PATH so you can type the bare command:

```powershell
.\scripts\install.cmd -AddToPath
```

It writes **only** `HKCU\Environment\Path` (never `HKLM`), backs the previous value up to `<install dir>\path-backup.txt` first, and does nothing if the directory is already listed. **Open a new terminal** for the change to take effect. `-Uninstall` also removes that PATH entry, so uninstalling does not leave a dead entry behind (the previous value is backed up again, this time into `%TEMP%`).
Without this step the installer does not touch your PATH at all, so keep using the full path `& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\AI-Terminal-Pet\AI-Terminal-Pet.exe" --json`.

The installer lives under `scripts/` rather than at the repository root on purpose: market indexers fetch a root `install.ps1` by name and regex-scan it, and this script legitimately mentions the `HKCU` Run key and a `-Recurse -Force` cleanup. Moving it one level down takes those two false positives off the root without taking any behaviour off the script.

Run `ai-terminal-pet --doctor` at any point after installing to self-check the environment, install files, runtime state, pipe, autostart entry, and node availability. To remove the deployed artifacts, run `.\scripts\install.cmd -Uninstall`; it asks for a typed `yes` confirmation first, refuses unsafe target directories, and accepts `-Force` for unattended removal.

Installing a terminal hook is required for that terminal to report; see the next section to connect your tools.

### Connect your terminal

| Terminal | How to connect | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| OpenCode | Add `file:///C:/path/to/ai-terminal-pet/reporters/opencode.js` to `plugins` in `opencode.json` (OpenCode 2.x: the file is a plugin with an `id` and a `setup`) | Turn, tool and permission states, including the difference between "waiting for you" and "still working" |
| Claude Code | Add `& "%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\pet-hook.exe" --mode=claude` for `SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `Stop`, and `Notification` in `settings.json`. `node <repo>/reporters/claude-hook.js` still works and is the fallback when you cannot run the `.exe`. | Real-time status updates, tool execution tracking, and permission prompt alerts |
| Antigravity | Set `statusLine.command` to `pet-statusline.exe` and configure `pet-hook.exe --mode=antigravity` for agent and tool events (`antigravity-hook.js` is the fallback) | Fast statusline updates, agent state changes, and permission request forwarding |
| DeepSeek Harness | Install the Cordis bundle from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\bundles\ai-terminal-pet-bridge\` via the plugin manager (`install_bundle`) | turn/start to working, tool/call to tool_use, approval/asked to waiting_permission, tool/result with an error to error, turn/end to idle, process exit to closed |
| Anything else | Run `node reporters/generic.js` with `--source`, `--state`, and `--project` flags | Instant status reporting from any custom script or CLI tool |

Writing your own reporter for a tool that is not listed here needs no source reading: [docs/PROTOCOL.md](docs/PROTOCOL.md) specifies the wire protocol (fields, state semantics, pipe-name derivation, acknowledgment contract, and redaction rules) that a conforming reporter must implement.

The Harness side is a host-only Cordis bundle: it holds no pipe-name, state-set or snapshot logic of its own, it loads the protocol from `%LOCALAPPDATA%\AI-Terminal-Pet\protocol.js` and delegates everything to it.

The Harness side has a second, self-contained option since `dsh-ai-terminal-pet` `1.1.0`: a standalone DSH plugin package at [`packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet`](packages/dsh-ai-terminal-pet), also shipped as a GitHub Release asset. evidence.readmeExcerpt:
# dsh-md-panel

右侧栏的「知识库」面板：把本地 Markdown 知识库（默认 `/mnt/Remotedata/Appdata/KnowledgeBase/KB`）变成 DSH 里随手可翻、随手可问的一块面板 —— 聊天在左，知识库在右，边读边问。

## 它能干什么

- **右侧栏入口**：
  - 会话标题右侧多一个书本按钮，点一下把「知识库」页开在右栏（页签与 Chat / Trajectory / Agent Browser 并列）；
  - 右栏的「+」引导页里也有「知识库」胶囊；
  - 实现是标准两阶段注册：`ctx.sidebarRightTabs.register({ id: 'dsh-md-panel', kind: 'kbPanel', … })` 定义页类型，正文挂 `sidebar.right.pane.tab`、标题挂 `sidebar.right.pane.tab.title`。
- **目录可收起**：面板顶栏「◀ 收起 / ☰ 目录」；宽屏（≥720px）目录与正文左右并排，窄屏上下叠（目录最多占 44% 高）。收起状态记在 `localStorage`（`dsh-md-panel:side-collapsed`），下次打开还是上次那个样子。
- **实时同步**：宿主每 2 秒扫一次文件指纹（路径 + 大小 + mtime），有变化就 SSE 推给浏览器。存盘即刷新，当前打开的那篇会静默重载，不用手动点刷新。
- **五种视图**：栏目树 / 全文搜索（命中行高亮）/ 最近更新 / 收藏（`localStorage`）/ 待补 frontmatter。
- **Markdown 预览**：标题锚点、大纲、表格、代码块、任务列表、`[[wiki]]` 与相对链接（面板内跳转）、`95-素材/` 图片（走 `/md-panel/api/asset`）。
- **frontmatter 徽章**：type / status / updated / tags，其余字段也摊开显示；缺 `type`、`updated`、`status` 会亮黄点并提示（跟 `dsh-kb-guard` 同一套规则）。
- **出链 / 反向链接**：谁引用了这篇、这篇又指向谁，一眼看得到。
- **接入对话（默认走当前会话）**：所有提问默认**追加进当前正在跑的这个会话的输入栏**，不打断手头对话、不另开会话。机制：在 `conversation.input.left` 挂一个不渲染的桥接组件拿会话的 `inputActions`，用 `captureInsertion()` + `insertText()` 插到光标处——不会覆盖你已经打的字，插不上就退回复制剪贴板。
  - 文档右上「引用」→ 只放这篇的引用（标题 + 相对路径 + 绝对路径）；
  - 文档右上「解读」→ 放引用 + 整篇解读要求（先读原文、列关键事实和坑）；
  - 选中正文任意一段 → 浮动条「解读这段 / 继续分析 / 总结」，带上所选原文一起放进输入栏；
  - 底部输入框「问小鲸鱼」→ 针对这篇问一句，回车即放进输入栏。
  - 底部输入框右侧「新会话提问」→ 唯一会**另开一个会话**的按钮：先弹一个工作区选择（当前工作区 / 其他工作区 / 跟随当前工作区），选定后**先让 DSH 开新会话、等新会话挂上来再往它的输入栏写**问题——分两步是因为 `startSession(workspaceId, { prompt })` 的草稿初始化会落在「当前仍保留的那个会话」上，实测会把问题写进旧会话的输入栏（新会话根本没建）。现在改成 `startSession(workspaceId)`（不带 options）+ 每 150ms 轮询桥接组件拿到的 `sessionId`，变了才 `insertText`；6 秒还没切过去就退回复制剪贴板并提示。
  - 所有路径**只填草稿不替你发**，改一句再按回车。
- **其他**：复制绝对路径、复制 `[[wiki]]` 链接、在系统文件管理器打开所在目录。

## 配置

`cordis.patch.yml` 里那几行：

```yaml
config:
  root: /mnt/Remotedata/Appdata/KnowledgeBase/KB
  pollIntervalMs: 2000
  verbose: false
```

- `root`：知识库根目录（`~` 不展开，写绝对路径）。
- `pollIntervalMs`：扫描间隔，默认 2000ms，夹在 500–60000 之间。
- `verbose`：调试日志开关。

改完 `plugin_manager` 里重启该插件即可生效。

## 宿主接口

全部挂在 `/md-panel/api` 下（同源，无鉴权，只读本地知识库 + 一个打开文件管理器的动作）：

| 方法 | 路径 | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/tree` | 全量索引：文件元数据、栏目、type/tag 统计、合规问题数 |
| GET | `/file?path=` | 单篇：frontmatter、正文、出链、反向链接 |
| GET | `/search?q=&limit=` | 全文搜索，带命中行 |
| GET | `/timeline?limit=` | 按 mtime 排序的最近变更 |
| GET | `/asset?path=` | 图片等素材（限知识库目录内） |
| GET | `/events` | SSE：`hello` / `change` 事件 |
| GET | `/status` | 扫描统计 |
| POST | `/rescan` | 立即重扫 |
| POST | `/open` | `{ path, mode: 'reveal' \| 'file' }` → 打开文件管理器 |

所有 `path` 参数都会被夹在 `root` 里面，`..` 越界直接 400。

## 仓库

GitHub（主，公开）：<https://github.com/kakarin/dsh-md-panel>

```bash
git clone https://github.com/kakarin/dsh-md-panel.git
git clone git@github.com:kakarin/dsh-md-panel.git      # SSH
```

内网 Gitea（镜像，公开）：<http://192.168.100.211:3000/rinzhao/dsh-md-panel>

```bash
git clone gitea:rinzhao/dsh-md-panel.git          # SSH 别名，见 ~/.ssh/config
git clone http://192.168.100.211:3000/rinzhao/dsh-md-panel.git   # HTTP
```

## 结构

```
dsh-md-panel/
├── package.json        # dsh.bundle.patch + dsh.client
├── cordis.patch.yml    # 插进 profile 的那一行（含 config）
├── icon.svg
├── locale/{zh,en}.json # meta.title / meta.description
└── lib/
    ├── index.js        # 宿主：索引、扫描、SSE、HTTP
    └── client.js       # 浏览器：右栏页类型 + 面板正文（手写 bundle，只 require react）
```

## 装 / 卸

```bash
# 装（在当前会话里）
plugin_manager action: install_bundle target=<本目录绝对路径>

# 卸
plugin_manager action: remove_bundle target=dsh-md-panel
```

## 注意

- 扫描会跳过工具目录与第三方仓库：`.git`、`.obsidian`、`.plume`、`node_modules`、`repos/`、`vendor/`、`third_party/`、`dist/`、`build/` 等——塞在知识库里的 ESP32 仓库不会污染文件树和「待补 frontmatter」计数。
- 面板只**读**知识库，不提供写入；改文档还是用编辑器 / Obsidian。这样不会跟 `dsh-kb-guard` 的写入校验打架。
- 全文搜索是宿主侧线性扫（500 篇量级几十毫秒），知识库到几万篇时需要换索引。

The native lib host/client browse and send knowledge excerpts into sessions; an open-file action invokes a detached process. package MIT is declared but repository license text is missing. No versioned DSH contract was found. The patch also contains an environment-specific /mnt knowledge root. No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.

evidence.readmeExcerpt:
Mistral Vibe is an unofficial DSH provider route for Mistral's Vibe Code subscription.
PKCE browser sign-in · the real Vibe and Studio/API meters · prices on every model · a live Session cost.

Features · Install · Images · Routes · Notes & limits

It registers the LLM route `mistral-vibe` against `https://api.mistral.ai/v1`, signs you in with the console's own PKCE flow, and — unlike the bundle it grew out of — shows the **real allowance meters** for the Vibe Code budget and the Studio/API budget. > Community integration, not affiliated with Mistral. Your own Mistral account's > plan and terms apply; usage made through this route is billed by Mistral to the > same allowance the Vibe CLI draws on. ## Features | | Feature | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | 🔐 | **PKCE browser sign-in** | Settings → *Mistral Vibe* → *Sign in with Mistral* runs `console.mistral.ai/api/vibe/sign-in`, opens the approval page, polls the process and, once approved, stores the minted key directly in the credential store. No copy-paste. | | 📊 | **Two real meters** | `GET /v1/billing/budget` returns the Vibe Code allowance and the Studio/API allowance separately; the account card draws both, with percent, used-of-total, currency and reset date. `GET /v1/billing/subscription` supplies the plan name. | | 📈 | **The meters in the sidebar** | The same two allowances sit in the sidebar foot, directly above the account row: dollars used of the allowance, its percentage, and a bar, with the reset date in the tooltip. Click to re-read; it also refreshes itself every ten minutes. | | 🗂️ | **A live catalogue** | `/v1/models` fills the picker; rows the key cannot use are kept visible but marked, so a `tier_not_allowed` 403 is a badge, not a mid-turn surprise. | | 💵 | **Prices on the model rows** | Every catalogue model shows its own price line — `$0.30 in · $0.007 cached · $1.20 out / 1M tokens` for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, taken from Mistral's model card — so the cost of a model is visible before you pick it. A model discovered at runtime has no published price and shows no line. | | 🧮 | **A price badge and a session cost run** | The picker badges each model with its input/output price (`$0.3/$1.2`), and the composer's token-usage pill — the one reading `27.3M tok · Cache hit 99%` — gains `· ≈$1.51` at the end of its own text run for the Session you are in. Folded from that Session's `assistant/message` usage at list prices, so a model switch mid-session prices each message on the model that actually ran it. | | 🧠 | **Per-model thinking levels** | Mapped onto `reasoning_effort`, with reasoning streamed as a thinking block rather than as text. | | 🖼️ | **Screenshots that do not wreck the cache** | Downscaled to 1024px / 768 KB, capped at Mistral's 20-image ceiling through the harness's durable offload protocol, and kept visible by default so a visual workflow can compare one render against the next. See [Images](#images). | | 🔑 | **Secrets stay out of YAML** | Keys live in the credential record named by `apiKeyEnv` (`MISTRAL_API_KEY` by default); the row keeps only a reference. | ## Install The package is **not published on npm yet**, so install it from the repository. `dsh plugin` forwards its arguments to `pnpm` inside the profile directory, which means any spec pnpm accepts works — a path, `file:`, `github:owner/repo`, or a published version. **From the repository:** ```sh dsh plugin --profile add github:Khuraie/dsh-mistral-vibe-provider ``` **From a clone** — what a development setup wants, because the profile links the checkout and an edit is live after a restart: ```sh git clone https://github.com/Khuraie/dsh-mistral-vibe-provider dsh plugin --profile add ./dsh-mistral-vibe-provider ``` `dsh plugin` only installs the dependency. The launcher stacks the patch layers listed in `dsh.profile.bundles`, so add the package name there too — in `~/.dsh/profiles//package.json`: ```json "dsh": { "profile": { "bundles": ["…", "@khuraie/dsh-mistral-vibe-provider"] } } ``` The in-app plugin manager does both steps in one go. Restart DSH afterwards. Then **Settings → Mistral Vibe** and either sign in with Mistral or paste a Vibe Code API key. Hit **Fetch available models** to persist the live catalogue, and **Refresh** on the account card to re-read the meters. The two meters also appear in the sidebar foot above the account row, so the remaining allowance is visible without opening Settings. Once the package is published, the shortest form becomes `dsh plugin --profile add @khuraie/dsh-mistral-vibe-provider`. ## Images Screenshots are the one input that can wreck Mistral's prompt cache, so this route manages them rather than forwarding whatever the harness hands it. The cache is a longest-common-prefix cache: it only serves a request that repeats the previous one byte for byte, and an image payload is the biggest thing that can change. ### Downscaling Every image is re-encoded before it is sent: **1024px** on the longest edge, **768 KB** encoded. In a measured Session, steps carrying a 1–4 MB screenshot fell to 1–26% cache hit while text-only steps in the same Session stayed at 86–100%. The harness default for other providers is 1568px / 4 MB; this route trades that detail for cache. | setting | default | effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `imageMaxEdge` | `1024` | longest edge, in pixels, of the image sent | | `imageMaxBytesKb` | `768` | encoded byte budget for one request image | ### The 20-image ceiling Mistral refuses a request carrying more than **20 images** — `400 invalid_request_invalid_args`, "Total number of images exceeds the maximum allowed of 20", code 3051. The route does not drop images itself: that would rewrite the transcript on every request and break the prefix cache. Instead it fails the step with `IMAGE_OFFLOAD_REQUIRED` and the count it needs, and the harness's `dsh-compaction-image-offload` plugin records one durable `image/offload` selection before retrying. The count is retired **four at a time**, so the retained window stays between 17 and 20 images instead of collapsing to one. An offloaded image becomes a named placeholder rather than a silent gap: ```text [image omitted from this request to stay inside the image limit (not a failed read); "render-04.png" (sha256:…)] ``` The "not a failed read" wording is load-bearing: without it a model finds the placeholder where its own `read_image` result used to be and reports the read as broken, then re-reads the file. ### Keeping images visible By default images stay on the wire up to the ceiling, because a visual workflow — render, look, edit, re-render — needs the previous render to compare against. `offloadSeenImages` is the **opt-in** cache mode, off by default the way Command Code ships its equivalent: once the model has answered on an image, that image becomes a placeholder, so a new screenshot no longer rolls the cache back. The cost is that seeing an old image again means reading it again. | setting | default | effect | | --- | --- | --- | | `offloadSeenImages` | `false` | opt-in: retire images the model has already answered on | | `imageKeepBatches` | `3` | in that mode, how many recent image batches keep their pixels | ### Measured | Session | images | offloads | cache efficiency | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 52-image judging, batch-cap design | 52 | 4 | 78.8% | | 192-step visual iteration, current default | 40 | 17 (2 after the fix) | **95.4%** | Keeping images and letting the budget retire four at a time measured *better* than the aggressive offloading it replaced: fewer transcript rewrites means more of the prefix survives. ## Routes | route | effect | | --- | --- | | `GET/POST /mistral-vibe/config` | the row as the page needs it (no key values) | | `POST /mistral-vibe/discover` | merge a live `/v1/models` read into the stored list | | `GET /mistral-vibe/budget` | plan name plus the Vibe and Studio/API meters | | `GET /mistral-vibe/session-cost?sessionId=…` | what one Session's Mistral Vibe usage cost at list prices | | `POST /mistral-vibe/sign-in` | start a PKCE attempt, answer the console URL | | `GET /mistral-vibe/sign-in/status?processId=…` | poll an attempt; on approval stores the key | All routes are loopback/same-origin by default and accept a configured access token for an exposed web UI. ## Notes and limits - **Thinking is on by default.** Mistral's own default for a request that carries no `reasoning_effort` is *off*, and a plugin that simply forwards "no level chosen" ends up running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash with no reasoning trace at all. This route declares `high` as the default level for every model that can think (the official DeepSeek route does the same), so a fresh Session thinks unless you pick `off` in the model picker. - **Images are managed, not forwarded.** Downscaling, the 20-image ceiling, the durable offload protocol and the opt-in cache mode are all in [Images](#images) above. - **Sticky routing for the prefix cache.** Mistral's prompt cache lives on the backend instance that served a prefix, so a request routed to another instance misses even when the prefix is byte-identical — the whole-prefix drops that show up a few times per Session. Every request now carries `x-affinity: `, the same header Mistral's own Vibe CLI sends, so a Session stays on one instance. It is only sent to `*.mistral.ai` hosts and can be turned off with `sendAffinity: false`. - **Tier gating is server-side per model.** On a free plan the live catalogue simply omits paid models such as `deepseek-v4-1-flash-1017`, and calling one answers `403 {"type":"tier_not_allowed","code":"1910"}`. The picker marks rows that never appeared in a live read; nothing is hidden automatically. - **Thinking models answer with `content` as an array of typed blocks** (`{"type":"thinking",…}`), which this adapter normalises into reasoning deltas. - **`max_tokens` includes reasoning tokens**, so a small cap can end a turn before any answer text arrives. - The bundle is derived from **[dsh-mistral-vibe](https://github.com/meltartica/dsh-mistral-vibe)** by Meltartica (MIT): the wire adapter, catalogue, thinking-level contract and client shell are theirs. This bundle replaces its settings half with the account card and adds the sign-in and billing routes. See `NOTICE`. ## License MIT © 2026 Meltartica and Mars-Sea — see `LICENSE` and `NOTICE`.

decision.reason: Held for versioned DSH compatibility. The MIT Git source includes host/client and vendored schema helpers. NOTICE attributes the upstream Meltartica project and LICENSE includes both notices. PKCE login, API keys, model discovery and budget routes are present, but the fixed manifest and captured docs do not declare a versioned DSH target. No candidate code or lifecycle hooks were executed; runtime safety and compatibility are unproven.
