# PowerContext memory for dsh-pet

This host-only adapter adds optional long-term memory to a dsh-pet instance in DSH Web and Desktop.
It connects to an existing PowerContext Server. Use DSH `0.2.2-rc.1`, dsh-pet `0.4.8`,
and the adapter and Server from the same PowerContext release or checkout.

See the [DSH integration guide](https://github.com/oceanbase/powercontext/blob/master/docs/en/docs/integrations/dsh.md)
for setup, diagnostics, privacy, and how to disable the adapter or discard pending dialogue.

From the repository root, run `make js-test` for transport, retry, and archive checks.
With the pinned `dsh` CLI on PATH, run `make dsh-pet-runtime-test` to install the package into
an isolated profile and exercise real dsh-pet chat and PowerContext Server processing.
On macOS, set `DSH_PET_TEST_DESKTOP_APP="/Applications/DeepSeek Harness.app"` with the same command
to launch the installed Desktop app and run the scenario through its renderer.
To install dsh-pet from an existing pnpm cache, set both `DSH_PET_TEST_PNPM_STORE`
(the store directory before the version suffix) and `DSH_PET_TEST_PNPM_CACHE`.
The test uses a deterministic local model fixture; its three-arm replay reports request bytes
and latency for native recent history, the same window with PowerContext, and full history.
It does not measure model quality or billed provider cost.

# PowerContext

**Context that stays with the work — across sessions, agents, and people.**

[![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/powercontext)](https://pypi.org/project/powercontext/)
[![License Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-community-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.com/invite/74cF8vbNEs)
[![Ask DeepWiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ask-DeepWiki-147DFF)](https://deepwiki.com/oceanbase/powercontext)

*[English](README.md) · [中文](README_CN.md) · [日本語](README_JP.md)*

[Website](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/) · [Quickstart](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/) · [Manual startup](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/manual-start/) · [Integrations](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/) · [Benchmarks](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/benchmarks/) · [Interfaces](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/develop/interfaces/)

## What is PowerContext?

**PowerContext is an open-source context service for AI agents.** It keeps the durable part of your work — decisions, constraints, evidence, progress — outside any single conversation, so the next session, the next agent, or the next person can pick up from the current state instead of rereading the transcript.

You can use it as a ready-to-run Server or embed the same contracts in another application:

| Layer | What it owns | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core protocol | `Source`, `Artifact`, and `Trigger` contracts | Embedding PowerContext or adding a component |
| Builtin runtime | Memory, Handoff, Experience, and Skill services, scheduling, inference, and supported storage backends | Running the standard local Server |
| Server and integrations | HTTP/MCP, Python Client, CLI, Dashboard, and Agent plugins | Connecting an Agent or application |

Work rarely ends with whoever starts it. You hand a task to an agent, the agent gets part of the way, and later you or someone else takes over. The reasoning and current state often stay behind in that conversation. PowerContext moves them out of the conversation and into revisioned artifacts you can inspect:

![You and agents hand work off and continue with stored context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-workflow.svg)

Everything belongs to a **Scope** — one isolated Source journal, Memory lifecycle, review inbox, and Handoff history. A Scope ID selects data; it does not prove user identity, grant tool access, or authorize execution.

```text
Scope
├── Source journal    # evidence: prompts, documents, work contracts, task outcomes
├── Memory            # atomic-memory/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION — decisions, constraints, next steps
├── Review Inbox      # pending Experience and Skill candidates awaiting a decision
├── Handoff history   # handoff/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION — work continuity across sessions
└── Topic Memory      # extracted in the background from eligible Sources
```

For Kubernetes deployments with external OceanBase, see the [Helm chart and deployment guide](deploy/helm/powercontext/README.md).

*Recordings show the running Dashboard and native Desktop preview in their light themes, using synthetic demonstration records.*

### Memory — decisions and constraints that outlive a session

Memory is a revisioned Artifact family for reusable decisions, constraints, facts, state, and next steps. An entry is `active`, `forgotten`, `merged`, or `retired`. Forgetting one through `POST /v1/atomic-memory/lifecycle` takes it out of active recall while its content and history stay available and restorable, without advancing the content revision. Explicit Memory writes need no model at all; extraction from captured Sources needs a configured generation pipeline.

> "Don't refactor the old auth module — mobile is still using it."
> Context this expensive shouldn't depend on someone repeating it in every session.

![Dashboard in light mode: search project memories and inspect a saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-dashboard-demo.gif)

### Handoff — the current state, not the whole transcript

Handoff records work continuity as a four-step loop:

```text
Work Contract → Prepared Handoff → Acknowledgement → Task Outcome
```

`handoff_current_work` captures an inspected boundary and returns a temporary Prepared Handoff. Committing it creates a durable Revision only when the user wants a milestone. The receiver resolves the Handoff and records an Acknowledgement; a Task Outcome preserves the final status and checks as Source evidence. The [Handoff Report](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/workflows/use-handoff-report/) projects the latest Revision in each selected Scope — read-only, and it never rewrites Memory.

![Dashboard in light mode: open a Handoff and inspect its saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-dashboard-handoff.gif)

### Experience — what worked, reviewed before it is reused

An Experience records a situation, an action, an observed outcome, and a reusable lesson. It enters a scope-local Review Inbox as a pending Candidate. Review writes use `expected_version`, so a decision cannot silently apply after another writer changes the proposal. Approval writes an immutable Revision; rejection records a reason. Both are terminal, and only the approved current head takes part in recall — pending, rejected, and historical Revisions are excluded.

### Skill — a reviewed procedure, exported on purpose

A managed Skill holds a name, a discovery description, instructions, validation checks, and lineage. Approval does not install or execute it: an exact approved Revision must be exported explicitly before an Agent host can discover the host-local projection.

### Desktop — inspect project memory from a connected workspace

Connect to a Server, select an exact Scope, and search its memories. Open a result to read its saved revision, or save a note for the next session. The [Desktop preview](desktop/README.md) is intended for internal validation; signed distribution and platform release qualification remain separate work.

![Native Desktop in light mode: search project memories and read an exact saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-desktop-demo.gif)

[Operational metrics](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/observability/) expose dependency observations, processing freshness, and attempt latency, including a protected metrics-only endpoint for standalone background deployments.

## Why PowerContext?

- **Context lives outside the conversation.** Memory, Handoff, Experience, and Skill are server-side artifacts, not files inside one agent's home directory. Switch from Codex to Claude Code — or hand the work to a teammate — and the work travels with you.
- **Everything is revisioned and traceable.** Each Artifact is addressed as `FAMILY/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION`. The Artifact ID stays stable while approved replacements create later Revisions, and reading an exact reference returns that historical snapshot even after the family head advances.
- **Generation, review, and execution are separate steps.** A model proposes content, review approves a Revision, and export creates a host-local copy. None of those steps grants an Agent permission to execute instructions. See [Interfaces](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/develop/interfaces/) for what each surface exposes today.
- **Recall is bounded, not dumped.** `PreparedContext` selects configured sections from active Memory and approved Experience, with optional Profile snapshots and Topic Memory, then applies a shared byte budget and returns `ready` content or `empty`. Recalled content is history, not an instruction authority: the receiving Agent still follows current instructions and checks live workspace state.
- **Review before reuse.** Experience and Skill pass through a review decision that is terminal either way, and approval writes an immutable Revision. With access control enforced, approval requires `scope.review`. An authorized Agent can approve its own Candidate; [separate submission and review](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/workflows/review-candidates/#separate-agent-submission-from-review) with distinct identities and permissions when a person must decide.
- **One Server, several views of the same contract.** HTTP is the complete remote application contract. The Python Client gives typed access, MCP is a curated Agent-facing projection, and Core protocols let an application assemble its own Source, Artifact, and Trigger implementations.

### How it compares

The comparison assumes typical single-agent or host-local setups; exact behavior depends on how each system is deployed.

| | Re-reading chat history | RAG over transcripts | Host-local memory files | PowerContext |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Survives a new session | manual | yes | yes | yes |
| Survives switching agents | no | no | no | yes |
| Handing work to a person | manual | manual | manual | Handoff, first-class |
| Reusable procedure | no | no | prose only | Experience / Skill |
| Earlier revisions kept | no | depends on the index | only via git | immutable Revisions |
| Review before reuse | n/a | no | no | Review Inbox |
| Bounded recall for one turn | no | partial | no | `PreparedContext` byte budget |
| Inspectable outside the Agent | no | no | yes | yes |

## Proof it works

![LoCoMo accuracy and SWE-bench Pro input tokens per 100 tasks, comparing PowerContext with baselines](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-benchmark-summary.svg)

- **Long-conversation memory (LoCoMo; 1,540 scored questions across categories 1–4): 90.78% accuracy**, against 52.9% for full-context replay — **+37.88 points** over full context.
- **Coding tasks (SWE-bench Pro paired comparison): approximately 225.32 million input tokens per 100 tasks with PowerContext on, versus 302.18 million with it off** — approximately **25.4% fewer input tokens**, or 76.86 million fewer per 100 tasks.
- **Retrieval quality (LoCoMo Plus)**, native PowerContext against PowerContext with Jev candidate filtering after retrieval. Each model is used for both Memory extraction and answering; embeddings use `qwen3.7-text-embedding` (1024 dimensions):

  | Model | PowerContext | PowerContext + Jev | Difference |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | GPT-4o-mini | 40.855% | 49.78% | +8.925 points |
  | Qwen3.7-plus | 60.37% | 68.947% | +8.577 points |
  | GPT-4o | 65.082% | 69.28% | +4.198 points |

Full methods, results, and limitations: [benchmarks](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/benchmarks/). Two caveats we would rather state than bury: the six LoCoMo Plus scores above were supplied by the project owner, and their run artifacts are not publicly available for verification — the published instructions reproduce the harness, not those scores. Windows support is `experimental`.

## Quick start

If you want to manually configure and start PowerContext, see the [manual startup guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/manual-start/).

PowerContext keeps durable project context outside any single chat. A first run follows this path:

```text
Agent input → Source evidence → Memory / Topic Memory → PreparedContext → next session or Agent
```

PowerContext 1.5.1 includes an interactive setup wizard. You need Python 3.11+, Git, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/); uv can provision Python when needed. To connect an Agent, also install its CLI. In the wizard, choose Basic memory for explicit saves and recall without model APIs; Full memory requires separate Generation and Embedding API credentials. For a local Server without model APIs, see [Install and run](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/install-and-run/). macOS and Linux are supported; Windows support is `experimental`. To provision Python and uv automatically, use the [installation script](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/install-and-run/#install-with-the-recommended-script).

Choose the path that matches your goal:

| Goal | Choose | What you need |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Try explicit saves and recall | **Basic memory** | CLI and Server; no model API |
| Process Sources automatically and use Topic Memory or semantic retrieval | **Full memory** | Separate Generation and Embedding API credentials; schedules and Scope policies still apply |
| Learn the core workflows in Python | The first seven Jupyter tutorials | A repository checkout and `uv`; no model or API key |

### 1. Install and run the wizard

```bash
uv tool install --force "powercontext[cli,server]==1.5.1"
mkdir -p powercontext-config && cd powercontext-config
powercontext config init --language en --output .env
```

The wizard asks about storage, local or remote usage, memory capabilities, Dashboard/access, and Agent connections. SQLite is the simplest first storage choice; choose embedded seekdb only when you need it and can approve its dependency install.

The wizard writes `.env` and `.env.next-steps.md`. These files can contain credentials; do not commit them. Linux needs an available `systemd --user` manager for the personal service.

After saving `.env`, validate it and register the personal service:

```bash
powercontext config validate --env-file .env
powercontext service install --env-file .env
powercontext service status
```

The service keeps the Server running after you close the terminal. Load the generated environment file and check the connection:

```bash
set -a
. ./.env
set +a
powercontext ready
powercontext capabilities
```

Continue with `.env.next-steps.md` to create and bind the selected Scopes. Use the real `scope_id` returned by the creation request; a planned `codex-...` title is not an ID. Changing directories does not create isolation; use the same Server and Scope in the Dashboard and Agent. After editing `.env`, rerun `powercontext service install --env-file .env` to apply the updated settings. Then install the matching plugins and launch a new Agent session. The [complete walkthrough](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/) covers Codex and Claude Code, Dashboard login, SSH forwarding, HTTPS prerequisites, and observable acceptance checks. For example, the matching Codex installation is:

```bash
powercontext setup codex --ref powercontext-v1.5.1
powercontext doctor codex
```

Before sending the first message in a new Codex session, open `/hooks` and, when prompted, trust the PowerContext hooks. Without an enabled `UserPromptSubmit` hook, automatic prompt capture and recall do not run, even if MCP connects. See [first-session checks and recovery](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/codex/#first-session-hook-trust). After the first check below, use the [capability and trigger guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/#5-choose-your-next-workflow) to try all seven Artifact families, Source, and Tag. Basic memory needs no separate Server model API; the Agent still uses its own model.

### 2. Verify the first end-to-end result

This checks the path that makes PowerContext useful: Source capture → background processing → cross-session recall. In the new Agent session bound to the same Scope, send a concrete decision such as:

```text
We are designing the Aurora acceptance project. Use uv for Python dependencies and .env for configuration.
The first deployment runs on one Linux server, with a Mac connecting through an SSH tunnel.
Restate these constraints without changing any code.
```

If you enabled Dashboard, open the URL printed by the wizard; an empty Dashboard before capture is expected. Then:

1. Confirm that the prompt appears as a Source.
2. After the configured inspection interval and model processing, confirm that a related Topic Memory appears.
3. Send a related update and confirm that the new Source arrives and the topic content or revision history reflects it.
4. Start a new Agent session with the same Scope and ask for the Aurora decisions with citations.

`doctor codex` checks installation and connectivity only. Source capture does not by itself create Memory or Topic Memory, and processing can wait for configured schedules and model work. In Basic memory mode, explicitly ask the Agent to save a decision, then search for it in a new session; that does not test automatic extraction.

### 3. Explore Python first — no API key

The tutorials run from a repository checkout and take their dependencies from a `uv` dependency group, so they are not part of the `powercontext` package. From the repository root:

```bash
uv sync --locked --group notebooks
uv run --locked --group notebooks jupyter lab --notebook-dir=examples/jupyter
```

Start with [01 · Memory across sessions](examples/jupyter/01_memory_across_sessions.ipynb), then work through the [22 Chinese Jupyter tutorials, including a complete team workflow](examples/jupyter/README.md) to run Memory, context preparation, Handoff, Experience, Skill, and a real Agent step by step. The first seven tutorials need no model or API key.

### Common issues

- `doctor codex` verifies Codex installation and connectivity. To verify automatic memory, check that a real prompt becomes a Source, produces a Topic, evolves after a related prompt, and can be recalled in a new session using the same Scope.
- If Python dependency downloads are slow or fail, configure a package index for [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/configuration/indexes/) and retry.
- Choose **Full memory capabilities** to test automatic Memory and Topic Memory; this requires separate Generation and Embedding API credentials. An Agent subscription does not provide those Server credentials. Choose **Basic memory** to save and retrieve memories explicitly without additional model APIs.
- If seekdb needs installing, the wizard asks once and installs the dependency in the background.
- The optional recall-sufficiency gate records scope-local daily search effort and budget omissions for later policy evaluation. See the [configuration reference](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/configuration/) for its recording and failure behavior.
- For a Server on another machine, use HTTPS or follow the [remote connection guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/connect-remote-server/). Setup recognizes remote HTTP URLs from flags or environment variables and asks for explicit consent; automated setup uses `--allow-insecure-http`.

## Connect your Agent

Codex is `official`; other maintained hosts and Python Agent frameworks are `community`; Bub is `evaluation` only. These tags describe PowerContext integration maintenance and use. The [capability matrix](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/capabilities/) records which hosts are qualified, along with their supported features and availability.

# PowerContext **Context that stays with the work — across sessions, agents, and people.** [![PyPI version](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/powercontext)](https://pypi.org/project/powercontext/) [![License Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache_2.0-blue.svg)](LICENSE) [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/badge/Discord-community-5865F2?logo=discord&logoColor=white)](https://discord.com/invite/74cF8vbNEs) [![Ask DeepWiki](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ask-DeepWiki-147DFF)](https://deepwiki.com/oceanbase/powercontext) *[English](README.md) · [中文](README_CN.md) · [日本語](README_JP.md)* [Website](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/) · [Quickstart](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/) · [Manual startup](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/manual-start/) · [Integrations](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/) · [Benchmarks](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/benchmarks/) · [Interfaces](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/develop/interfaces/) ## What is PowerContext? **PowerContext is an open-source context service for AI agents.** It keeps the durable part of your work — decisions, constraints, evidence, progress — outside any single conversation, so the next session, the next agent, or the next person can pick up from the current state instead of rereading the transcript. You can use it as a ready-to-run Server or embed the same contracts in another application: | Layer | What it owns | Use it when | | --- | --- | --- | | Core protocol | `Source`, `Artifact`, and `Trigger` contracts | Embedding PowerContext or adding a component | | Builtin runtime | Memory, Handoff, Experience, and Skill services, scheduling, inference, and supported storage backends | Running the standard local Server | | Server and integrations | HTTP/MCP, Python Client, CLI, Dashboard, and Agent plugins | Connecting an Agent or application | Work rarely ends with whoever starts it. You hand a task to an agent, the agent gets part of the way, and later you or someone else takes over. The reasoning and current state often stay behind in that conversation. PowerContext moves them out of the conversation and into revisioned artifacts you can inspect: ![You and agents hand work off and continue with stored context](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-workflow.svg) Everything belongs to a **Scope** — one isolated Source journal, Memory lifecycle, review inbox, and Handoff history. A Scope ID selects data; it does not prove user identity, grant tool access, or authorize execution. ```text Scope ├── Source journal # evidence: prompts, documents, work contracts, task outcomes ├── Memory # atomic-memory/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION — decisions, constraints, next steps ├── Review Inbox # pending Experience and Skill candidates awaiting a decision ├── Handoff history # handoff/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION — work continuity across sessions └── Topic Memory # extracted in the background from eligible Sources ``` For Kubernetes deployments with external OceanBase, see the [Helm chart and deployment guide](deploy/helm/powercontext/README.md). *Recordings show the running Dashboard and native Desktop preview in their light themes, using synthetic demonstration records.* ### Memory — decisions and constraints that outlive a session Memory is a revisioned Artifact family for reusable decisions, constraints, facts, state, and next steps. An entry is `active`, `forgotten`, `merged`, or `retired`. Forgetting one through `POST /v1/atomic-memory/lifecycle` takes it out of active recall while its content and history stay available and restorable, without advancing the content revision. Explicit Memory writes need no model at all; extraction from captured Sources needs a configured generation pipeline. > "Don't refactor the old auth module — mobile is still using it." > Context this expensive shouldn't depend on someone repeating it in every session. ![Dashboard in light mode: search project memories and inspect a saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-dashboard-demo.gif) ### Handoff — the current state, not the whole transcript Handoff records work continuity as a four-step loop: ```text Work Contract → Prepared Handoff → Acknowledgement → Task Outcome ``` `handoff_current_work` captures an inspected boundary and returns a temporary Prepared Handoff. Committing it creates a durable Revision only when the user wants a milestone. The receiver resolves the Handoff and records an Acknowledgement; a Task Outcome preserves the final status and checks as Source evidence. The [Handoff Report](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/workflows/use-handoff-report/) projects the latest Revision in each selected Scope — read-only, and it never rewrites Memory. ![Dashboard in light mode: open a Handoff and inspect its saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-dashboard-handoff.gif) ### Experience — what worked, reviewed before it is reused An Experience records a situation, an action, an observed outcome, and a reusable lesson. It enters a scope-local Review Inbox as a pending Candidate. Review writes use `expected_version`, so a decision cannot silently apply after another writer changes the proposal. Approval writes an immutable Revision; rejection records a reason. Both are terminal, and only the approved current head takes part in recall — pending, rejected, and historical Revisions are excluded. ### Skill — a reviewed procedure, exported on purpose A managed Skill holds a name, a discovery description, instructions, validation checks, and lineage. Approval does not install or execute it: an exact approved Revision must be exported explicitly before an Agent host can discover the host-local projection. ### Desktop — inspect project memory from a connected workspace Connect to a Server, select an exact Scope, and search its memories. Open a result to read its saved revision, or save a note for the next session. The [Desktop preview](desktop/README.md) is intended for internal validation; signed distribution and platform release qualification remain separate work. ![Native Desktop in light mode: search project memories and read an exact saved revision](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-desktop-demo.gif) [Operational metrics](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/observability/) expose dependency observations, processing freshness, and attempt latency, including a protected metrics-only endpoint for standalone background deployments. ## Why PowerContext? - **Context lives outside the conversation.** Memory, Handoff, Experience, and Skill are server-side artifacts, not files inside one agent's home directory. Switch from Codex to Claude Code — or hand the work to a teammate — and the work travels with you. - **Everything is revisioned and traceable.** Each Artifact is addressed as `FAMILY/ARTIFACT_ID@REVISION`. The Artifact ID stays stable while approved replacements create later Revisions, and reading an exact reference returns that historical snapshot even after the family head advances. - **Generation, review, and execution are separate steps.** A model proposes content, review approves a Revision, and export creates a host-local copy. None of those steps grants an Agent permission to execute instructions. See [Interfaces](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/develop/interfaces/) for what each surface exposes today. - **Recall is bounded, not dumped.** `PreparedContext` selects configured sections from active Memory and approved Experience, with optional Profile snapshots and Topic Memory, then applies a shared byte budget and returns `ready` content or `empty`. Recalled content is history, not an instruction authority: the receiving Agent still follows current instructions and checks live workspace state. - **Review before reuse.** Experience and Skill pass through a review decision that is terminal either way, and approval writes an immutable Revision. With access control enforced, approval requires `scope.review`. An authorized Agent can approve its own Candidate; [separate submission and review](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/workflows/review-candidates/#separate-agent-submission-from-review) with distinct identities and permissions when a person must decide. - **One Server, several views of the same contract.** HTTP is the complete remote application contract. The Python Client gives typed access, MCP is a curated Agent-facing projection, and Core protocols let an application assemble its own Source, Artifact, and Trigger implementations. ### How it compares The comparison assumes typical single-agent or host-local setups; exact behavior depends on how each system is deployed. | | Re-reading chat history | RAG over transcripts | Host-local memory files | PowerContext | |---|---|---|---|---| | Survives a new session | manual | yes | yes | yes | | Survives switching agents | no | no | no | yes | | Handing work to a person | manual | manual | manual | Handoff, first-class | | Reusable procedure | no | no | prose only | Experience / Skill | | Earlier revisions kept | no | depends on the index | only via git | immutable Revisions | | Review before reuse | n/a | no | no | Review Inbox | | Bounded recall for one turn | no | partial | no | `PreparedContext` byte budget | | Inspectable outside the Agent | no | no | yes | yes | ## Proof it works ![LoCoMo accuracy and SWE-bench Pro input tokens per 100 tasks, comparing PowerContext with baselines](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oceanbase/powercontext/master/docs/assets/readme-benchmark-summary.svg) - **Long-conversation memory (LoCoMo; 1,540 scored questions across categories 1–4): 90.78% accuracy**, against 52.9% for full-context replay — **+37.88 points** over full context. - **Coding tasks (SWE-bench Pro paired comparison): approximately 225.32 million input tokens per 100 tasks with PowerContext on, versus 302.18 million with it off** — approximately **25.4% fewer input tokens**, or 76.86 million fewer per 100 tasks. - **Retrieval quality (LoCoMo Plus)**, native PowerContext against PowerContext with Jev candidate filtering after retrieval. Each model is used for both Memory extraction and answering; embeddings use `qwen3.7-text-embedding` (1024 dimensions): | Model | PowerContext | PowerContext + Jev | Difference | |---|---|---|---| | GPT-4o-mini | 40.855% | 49.78% | +8.925 points | | Qwen3.7-plus | 60.37% | 68.947% | +8.577 points | | GPT-4o | 65.082% | 69.28% | +4.198 points | Full methods, results, and limitations: [benchmarks](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/benchmarks/). Two caveats we would rather state than bury: the six LoCoMo Plus scores above were supplied by the project owner, and their run artifacts are not publicly available for verification — the published instructions reproduce the harness, not those scores. Windows support is `experimental`. ## Quick start If you want to manually configure and start PowerContext, see the [manual startup guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/manual-start/). PowerContext keeps durable project context outside any single chat. A first run follows this path: ```text Agent input → Source evidence → Memory / Topic Memory → PreparedContext → next session or Agent ``` PowerContext 1.5.1 includes an interactive setup wizard. You need Python 3.11+, Git, and [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/); uv can provision Python when needed. To connect an Agent, also install its CLI. In the wizard, choose Basic memory for explicit saves and recall without model APIs; Full memory requires separate Generation and Embedding API credentials. For a local Server without model APIs, see [Install and run](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/install-and-run/). macOS and Linux are supported; Windows support is `experimental`. To provision Python and uv automatically, use the [installation script](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/install-and-run/#install-with-the-recommended-script). Choose the path that matches your goal: | Goal | Choose | What you need | | --- | --- | --- | | Try explicit saves and recall | **Basic memory** | CLI and Server; no model API | | Process Sources automatically and use Topic Memory or semantic retrieval | **Full memory** | Separate Generation and Embedding API credentials; schedules and Scope policies still apply | | Learn the core workflows in Python | The first seven Jupyter tutorials | A repository checkout and `uv`; no model or API key | ### 1. Install and run the wizard ```bash uv tool install --force "powercontext[cli,server]==1.5.1" mkdir -p powercontext-config && cd powercontext-config powercontext config init --language en --output .env ``` The wizard asks about storage, local or remote usage, memory capabilities, Dashboard/access, and Agent connections. SQLite is the simplest first storage choice; choose embedded seekdb only when you need it and can approve its dependency install. The wizard writes `.env` and `.env.next-steps.md`. These files can contain credentials; do not commit them. Linux needs an available `systemd --user` manager for the personal service. After saving `.env`, validate it and register the personal service: ```bash powercontext config validate --env-file .env powercontext service install --env-file .env powercontext service status ``` The service keeps the Server running after you close the terminal. Load the generated environment file and check the connection: ```bash set -a . ./.env set +a powercontext ready powercontext capabilities ``` Continue with `.env.next-steps.md` to create and bind the selected Scopes. Use the real `scope_id` returned by the creation request; a planned `codex-...` title is not an ID. Changing directories does not create isolation; use the same Server and Scope in the Dashboard and Agent. After editing `.env`, rerun `powercontext service install --env-file .env` to apply the updated settings. Then install the matching plugins and launch a new Agent session. The [complete walkthrough](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/) covers Codex and Claude Code, Dashboard login, SSH forwarding, HTTPS prerequisites, and observable acceptance checks. For example, the matching Codex installation is: ```bash powercontext setup codex --ref powercontext-v1.5.1 powercontext doctor codex ``` Before sending the first message in a new Codex session, open `/hooks` and, when prompted, trust the PowerContext hooks. Without an enabled `UserPromptSubmit` hook, automatic prompt capture and recall do not run, even if MCP connects. See [first-session checks and recovery](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/codex/#first-session-hook-trust). After the first check below, use the [capability and trigger guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/get-started/quickstart/#5-choose-your-next-workflow) to try all seven Artifact families, Source, and Tag. Basic memory needs no separate Server model API; the Agent still uses its own model. ### 2. Verify the first end-to-end result This checks the path that makes PowerContext useful: Source capture → background processing → cross-session recall. In the new Agent session bound to the same Scope, send a concrete decision such as: ```text We are designing the Aurora acceptance project. Use uv for Python dependencies and .env for configuration. The first deployment runs on one Linux server, with a Mac connecting through an SSH tunnel. Restate these constraints without changing any code. ``` If you enabled Dashboard, open the URL printed by the wizard; an empty Dashboard before capture is expected. Then: 1. Confirm that the prompt appears as a Source. 2. After the configured inspection interval and model processing, confirm that a related Topic Memory appears. 3. Send a related update and confirm that the new Source arrives and the topic content or revision history reflects it. 4. Start a new Agent session with the same Scope and ask for the Aurora decisions with citations. `doctor codex` checks installation and connectivity only. Source capture does not by itself create Memory or Topic Memory, and processing can wait for configured schedules and model work. In Basic memory mode, explicitly ask the Agent to save a decision, then search for it in a new session; that does not test automatic extraction. ### 3. Explore Python first — no API key The tutorials run from a repository checkout and take their dependencies from a `uv` dependency group, so they are not part of the `powercontext` package. From the repository root: ```bash uv sync --locked --group notebooks uv run --locked --group notebooks jupyter lab --notebook-dir=examples/jupyter ``` Start with [01 · Memory across sessions](examples/jupyter/01_memory_across_sessions.ipynb), then work through the [22 Chinese Jupyter tutorials, including a complete team workflow](examples/jupyter/README.md) to run Memory, context preparation, Handoff, Experience, Skill, and a real Agent step by step. The first seven tutorials need no model or API key. ### Common issues - `doctor codex` verifies Codex installation and connectivity. To verify automatic memory, check that a real prompt becomes a Source, produces a Topic, evolves after a related prompt, and can be recalled in a new session using the same Scope. - If Python dependency downloads are slow or fail, configure a package index for [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/configuration/indexes/) and retry. - Choose **Full memory capabilities** to test automatic Memory and Topic Memory; this requires separate Generation and Embedding API credentials. An Agent subscription does not provide those Server credentials. Choose **Basic memory** to save and retrieve memories explicitly without additional model APIs. - If seekdb needs installing, the wizard asks once and installs the dependency in the background. - The optional recall-sufficiency gate records scope-local daily search effort and budget omissions for later policy evaluation. See the [configuration reference](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/configuration/) for its recording and failure behavior. - For a Server on another machine, use HTTPS or follow the [remote connection guide](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/operate/connect-remote-server/). Setup recognizes remote HTTP URLs from flags or environment variables and asks for explicit consent; automated setup uses `--allow-insecure-http`. ## Connect your Agent Codex is `official`; other maintained hosts and Python Agent frameworks are `community`; Bub is `evaluation` only. These tags describe PowerContext integration maintenance and use. The [capability matrix](https://powercontext.oceanbase.io/en/docs/integrations/capabilities/) records which hosts are qualified, along with their supported features and availability.

# DSH Community Market

[中文说明](README.zh.md)

DSH Community Market is the open plugin market built into [DSH Desktop](../README.en.md). It discovers plugins from user-selected catalog sources and performs simple npm package operations against the active Desktop Profile.

> A catalog listing or an installable result is not a security review, compatibility guarantee, or endorsement. Installed plugins run locally with the user's permissions.

The package declares a standard `dsh.bundle.patch`. Desktop Next exposes it in the official Plugins page alongside independently selectable dshmarket and Agents Anywhere. Stable/Beta retain their existing market selectors.

## Product behavior

The Market has four views:

1. **Discover** browses the selected source, with search, category filters, details, and source attribution.
2. **Installable** shows normalized entries that expose one unambiguous npm package identity. It does not trust a source-provided version.
3. **Installed** lists the active Profile's community plugins as the official plugin manager reports them, including plugins installed by this Market, another market, or the DSH CLI, and lets the user enable, disable, or uninstall them. Official plugins, bundles the installation ships, DeepSeek's own packages, and Desktop's built-in bundles (`dsh-community-market`, `dshmarket`, `@agents-anywhere/dsh-bridge-next`) are managed on the official Plugins page and do not appear here.
4. **Sources** saves, orders, and selects catalog sources. Exactly one source is active for browsing.

The Renderer never sends a package name or package-manager command for an installation. It submits the selected source and item identity, then the Host resolves the normalized package identity it previously observed.

## Automatic installation

Automatic installation deliberately has a small qualification boundary:

- the selected catalog entry exposes exactly one valid npm package name;
- the package is not a Desktop-owned product bundle;
- the official npm registry's `latest` endpoint returns the same package name and an exact stable version; and
- that npm manifest declares a valid `dsh.bundle.patch` path.

Source versions, verification badges, repository equality, deprecation metadata, lifecycle scripts, engine ranges, tarball integrity metadata, and build-allowance claims do not decide Market eligibility. pnpm remains responsible for resolving and installing the requested exact npm version.

After confirmation, the Host calls the official plugin manager's `installBundle` with the exact `name@version` target, saved exactly and activated. The manager validates the bundle, restores the Profile manifest and lockfile when installation fails, selects the bundle, and applies it live where the Host runs HMR. The Market creates no install receipt, snapshot, retry, cleanup, or rollback path of its own. When the manager reports that a restart is still required, the Market says so in its completion notice instead of prompting for one.

## Enable, disable, uninstall, and cross-market compatibility

The Installed view is derived from the official plugin manager's bundle list, not from Market receipts or the selected catalog. This makes plugins installed by external markets and the DSH CLI visible without special integration. The view keeps to community plugins: a bundle the manager marks official, a bundle the installation ships, a package in the `@deepseek-ai` scope, or one of Desktop's built-in bundles is left to the official Plugins page.

Enable and disable call the manager's `setBundleEnabled` directly and keep the dependency installed. Uninstall preview accepts a package name from that list; the Host confirms through the manager that the bundle is still removable before the preview and again before execution, then calls `removeBundle`, which deselects and unloads the bundle before pnpm removes it. The manager's `readOnlyReason`, `error`, and `removable` flags decide which actions a listed bundle offers.

## Catalog sources

Anyone may publish a source implementing the public [`catalog-source`](docs/schemas/catalog-source.schema.json) and [`catalog-provider-page`](docs/schemas/catalog-provider-page.schema.json) contracts. Existing APIs can be integrated through reviewed local adapters. Remote source data is normalized before the Client sees it, and provider commands are never displayed or executed.

[DSH 1024Store](https://github.com/imsai-sh/awesome-deepseek-harness-plugins) is an optional cooperating source. Desktop uses its current paginated `/api/v2/plugins` directory for browsing, search, sorting, and categories instead of the frozen 500-item v1 compatibility feed. The v2 command is never executed: an exact plain `dsh plugin --profile … add <npm-package>` shape contributes only the npm package identity, and npm `latest` remains the version authority during install preview. Browse-only GitHub targets remain visible without being marked automatically installable.

[dshfind](https://dshfind.com) is another optional cooperating source. Its adapter walks the provider's versioned REST pages and normalizes structured npm identity without executing provider command text. Any provider-supplied version remains informational; automatic installation still resolves npm `latest`.

Source requests are HTTPS-only, credential-free, bounded, and protected against unsafe redirects and private-network destinations. A source failure never changes the user's selected source or blocks DSH Desktop startup.

## Manual installation

When automatic installation is unavailable, the details dialog may show a bounded, display-only npm command reconstructed by the Host. **Open DSH Terminal** only opens Desktop's terminal; it does not paste or execute the command.

If an automatic installation starts but the official manager reports a failure, the Market records the manager's bounded pnpm output in the Desktop log and shows the same diagnostic output in a failure dialog. The dialog offers a Host-derived exact command and **Open DSH Terminal** for manual follow-up; it never retries the consumed confirmation automatically.

## Documentation

- [Install and uninstall](docs/install-and-uninstall.md)
- [Market shell](docs/market-shell.md)
- [Catalog provider contract](docs/catalog-provider-contract.md)
- [Catalog adapter guide](docs/catalog-adapter-guide.md)
- [Security](SECURITY.md)
- [Desktop plugin services](../dsh-plugin-desktop/docs/plugin-services.md)

## License and attribution

Package code and documentation are licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE). No third-party catalog snapshot, provider command, or artwork is bundled in this package. Catalog providers remain independent projects responsible for their own metadata and service policies.

# OmniMux Client

OmniMux 桌面客户端与产品插件的单一代码仓库。

**属于你的内容电商团队** —— 一套内容电商系统与桌面 Agent 工作台，用于可带货视频拆解、商品/人物资产创建、参考视频复刻与定时发布。

## 目录

```text
app/        Electron 桌面壳（deepseek-harness 之上），含 dsh-desktop-next、dsh-plugin-desktop、
            dsh-community-fabric、dsh-community-market、patches、assets、config、docs
plugins/    产品插件（omnimux 及 20 个能力插件、3 个共享包），随桌面版一起发布
```

两个子项目在**阶段一各自独立**：`app/` 用 Yarn 4，`plugins/` 用 pnpm。统一成单一 pnpm workspace 是下一步，届时才有一个根 lockfile。

## 构建

```bash
# 插件
cd plugins && corepack pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && corepack pnpm -r build

# 桌面壳
cd app && corepack enable && corepack yarn install --immutable && corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next dist:mac
```

`app/deepseek-harness` 是 submodule，pin 记录在 `PROVENANCE.json`；首次检出后执行
`git submodule update --init app/deepseek-harness`。

## 来源与追溯

本仓首次导入时由两份**已公开**的源码树合成，逐项记录在 [`PROVENANCE.json`](./PROVENANCE.json)：

| 目录 | 来源仓 | 导入 commit |
|---|---|---|
| `app/` | 私有桌面开发仓（已归档只读） | `70324365` |
| `plugins/` | `omnimux-ai/omnimux-dsh` | `1ec38f08a` |

私有开发历史不带入本仓；旧仓只读归档。

## 不在本仓

- **服务端网关**（Go，new-api fork）：[`omnimux-ai/omnimux-gateway`](https://github.com/omnimux-ai/omnimux-gateway)，仅因 AGPL 义务公开
- 托管服务的渠道凭据、定价账本、部署与运维物料：私有仓，不公开

## 许可

OmniMux 部分为 AGPL-3.0。上游组件保留其原始许可：桌面壳基于 [anywhere-labs/deepseek-harness-desktop](https://github.com/anywhere-labs/deepseek-harness-desktop)（MIT），harness 为 [deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness)（MIT），插件网关部分基于 [QuantumNous/new-api](https://github.com/QuantumNous/new-api)。详见各处 `LICENSE` 与 `NOTICE`。

# DSH NEXT

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

A separate experimental package based on DeepSeek Harness **0.1.6-alpha.2**. The main window loads the official published `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-frontend`, sharing the official Web application, plugin manager, and basic Desktop presentation. Next adds the system tray, desktop preferences and tools, Profiles, recovery, Agents Anywhere remote control, Community Market, and dshmarket.

## Development and verification

Run from the outer repository root with Node.js `^22.19.0` or `>=24.0.0` and Corepack's Yarn 4.18.0:

```sh
git submodule update --init --recursive
corepack yarn install --immutable
corepack yarn check:next
corepack yarn dev:next
```

`check:next` builds Market and Next, runs typechecks, unit tests, official-frontend and sandboxed-preload checks, and a real Host smoke in a temporary home. It never opens a graphical application. The smoke uses an offline local fixture plugin to exercise pnpm, Market toggles and removal through the official plugin manager, authentication, profile switching, and recovery boot, then cleans up its processes and files. An additional real-runtime smoke exercises the native-only HTTP/WebSocket gate, browser access changes, corrupt manifests, isolated safe mode, global-patch repair, and process teardown.

`dev:next` explicitly launches the graphical application. Use `corepack yarn start:next` with an existing build. Both prepare the bundled interpreter payload under `.desktop-build/runtime` before the shell starts, as upstream Desktop's development launcher does, so the Office skills are available in development; the first launch downloads the locked archives and wheels. An uncached Electron binary is downloaded on first use. To additionally exercise the real Electron executable in Node mode, build first and run:

```sh
corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next verify:host:electron
```

This check opens no Electron window. Window presentation, native dialogs, and a real phone connection still require manual acceptance.

CI also runs `xvfb-run --auto-servernum corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next verify:protocol --no-sandbox` on Linux. This separate test uses a real Electron renderer and custom protocol with a temporary Host, exercises Market source changes with ordinary browser access disabled, and rejects requests from a different page origin. It is not part of the portable `check:next` command. The sandbox flag applies only to the isolated CI process.

On the same Linux/Xvfb runner, `verify:sidebar-browser --no-sandbox` checks real lease-gated guest pages against a local fixture with both `frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`. It verifies blocked iframe embedding, successful native loading, the guest's own security settings, app-cookie and preload isolation, native history, refusal of a forged lease, workspace partition separation and cleanup on release. The portable `verify:window-controls` check exercises the official toolbar, pane resizing, modal overlap, tab switching and closure with a simulated native bridge, and checks the iframe fallback in a regular Web client.

The macOS sidebar and titlebar regression runs the official frontend's Desktop boot branch in headless Chromium with a temporary home. It serves the same entry document as Next, supplies real Host injections through a simulated preload contract, and asserts that Desktop transport is active. It checks the official header before Workspace selection and after a real blank Session is created, sidebar reopening on the homepage and plugin list/detail pages, and the official `data-window-drag` rows. Window resizing and sidebar collapse preserve the conversation header's drag surface; modal portals and interactive controls retain the official drag exclusions. It also opens the Desktop settings section inside the official Settings dialog, verifies preference and Profile commands, and renders the exact standalone recovery artifact with no Host dependency. Native IPC is simulated for these browser checks. After building, install the test browser once and run:

```sh
corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next exec playwright install chromium
corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next verify:window-controls
corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next verify:onboarding
```

Set `DSH_NEXT_TEST_BROWSER_CHANNEL=chrome` to use an installed Google Chrome instead. Screenshots are saved under `dsh-desktop-next/.desktop-next/verification/`. Native macOS window movement still needs manual verification. Next uses the official frontend's window drag ownership, interactive-control exclusions, modal portal geometry, and Electron region-recall watcher. The conversation header and plugin page headers own their draggable boxes. The official frame places the sidebar and new-session controls beside the macOS traffic lights. Next adds no title-row drag override, fixed caption band, sidebar-control positioning, or modal/fullscreen drag override.

## App icon resources

`build/app-icon.icon` is the editable Icon Composer project with the final NEXT badge layout and System Dark background. On macOS with Xcode 27 and Icon Composer, run `corepack yarn icons:export --channel next` from the repository root to refresh `build/app-icon.png`, the Windows `build/app-icon.ico`, native compiler output `build/app-icon.icns`, and the development Dock image `build/app-icon-mac.png`. Commit these files and `build/app-icon.resources.json` together; `corepack yarn icons:check` verifies them headlessly on any OS.

Next macOS packaging consumes the layered `.icon` source and compiles `Assets.car`, as Stable and Beta do. The raster Dock image is used only during unpackaged development; Windows and Linux windows use their ICO and PNG exports respectively.

## Usage

Use **Settings → Desktop settings** in the official frontend. A notice at the top links to the **Plugins** page for plugin-market and remote-control settings; it closes Settings and opens Plugins in the same main window. The tray’s **Settings…** entry and `CmdOrCtrl+,` reveal the main window and open the same official Settings dialog; there is no separate settings window. Recovery and Profile tools retain their existing windows. If the Host fails, the settings shortcut opens the recovery assistant. Switching Profiles saves the selection and fully relaunches the application after the old Host stops. Port changes restart only the Host; both interrupt active tasks. Browser and LAN access toggles apply immediately without restarting.

- **Tray and background operation:** retain the original Desktop ordering: open the main window, reload the interface, quit and restart, open DSH Terminal, export diagnostics, enter/exit safe mode, then select or create a Profile. Desktop settings and the recovery assistant remain directly accessible. Native menus follow the in-app language. Closing the main window keeps the Host and remote connection running when background operation is enabled and a tray is available. Explicit Quit and application relaunch first hide the existing windows, then wait for the HTTPS edge and Host to stop before exiting or relaunching. Restarting only the Host retains the main window. Without a usable tray, closing the main window quits rather than leaving an inaccessible process.
- **Sidebar browser:** the desktop app reuses the official Browser toolbar and supplies isolated Electron `WebContentsView` pages. GitHub and other sites with anti-framing policies can load as top-level pages without removing CSP or `X-Frame-Options`. Native history and observed URLs drive Back, Forward and the address bar. Views follow pane bounds and zoom, leave resize handles accessible, hide beneath modals or overlapping panes, and close with their tab or renderer. Each tab uses an in-memory session without the app preload, app cookies, Node access, downloads or automatic permission grants. Ordinary Web clients retain the official iframe carrier.
- **Desktop preferences:** background operation, macOS transparency, local/LAN access, log level, and separate notifications for completed/failed user turns. Background jobs never send notifications. The page reuses the existing Desktop grouped cards, Profile choices and notification toggles. Toggles and materials save immediately. The official Settings header provides terminal and restart shortcuts, including reload, application restart and restart into recovery. As in the existing Desktop, Windows has no material choice and always uses an opaque window; old Acrylic or Mica preferences are read as off. The OS must also allow notifications. Notifications only appear while the main window is unfocused. Successful turns use the current user message as the title and the final visible assistant reply as the body, with bounded text previews. Failed turns use a generic status; subagents and automated turns do not notify.
- **Profiles:** fresh installations and isolated safe mode use `desktop` by default. A saved selection is retained, including an older Profile named `default`; existing Profile directories are not renamed or overwritten. Create, switch, open, or remove an inactive Profile. New Profile from the tray focuses the name and offers creation followed by switching. Malformed manifests and Profiles missing the Next bundle are marked unavailable; selecting the already-active Profile does not restart it. Removed Profiles move into recovery backups; the active Profile and `desktop` cannot be removed. Profiles have separate plugin dependencies, activation lists and patches. Sessions, settings and credentials follow upstream rules and are shared within one Next home; Profiles do not isolate accounts or data.
- **First-run setup:** Desktop setup runs first when its own per-Profile completion record or explicit reopen request requires it. A lightweight standalone welcome window opens before the Host starts, rendering the six-page Next onboarding flow: welcome, plugin market, remote control, Computer Use (including the existing permission dialog), browser access, and recovery guidance. Back retains draft choices; Finish saves the Profile features, browser access preference, and Computer Use provider, records completion last, starts the Host once with those choices, and opens the main window; Skip preserves existing choices and starts the Host. When the main window opens, the continuation slot offers the DeepSeek account sign-in card (after completion) and then hands off to the official account onboarding, which independently evaluates its account, API-key, and saved-progress conditions. Neither flow completes or resets the other. Interrupted flows resume, completed Profiles do not repeat automatically, and safe/recovery modes bypass Desktop setup. Desktop settings → Desktop tools → Setup wizard can reopen it with current choices through a confirmed restart.
- **Markets:** plugin markets are off by default for new Profiles. The switch at the top of the official **Plugins** page enables or disables the last selected market (or `dsh-community-market` if none was selected in this view); choose `dsh-community-market` or `dshmarket` there. The choices reuse the original Desktop names, descriptions and repository links. Choosing one disables the other in a single official plugin-manager operation and retains installed plugins. Community Market keeps its sidebar entry; dshmarket keeps **Settings → Plugin Market**. Community Market retains discovery, sources, installation previews, confirmation, enable and disable switches, and removal. Package operations run through the official plugin manager and apply live without a restart; the terminal action is available on macOS and Windows.
- **Remote control:** the separate switch at the top of **Plugins** enables `@agents-anywhere/dsh-bridge-next` (off by default). The gear to its left opens the existing phone connection dialog, also available from the sidebar. The gear becomes available after enablement. AA uses its default state directory (`~/.agents-anywhere/dsh-bridge-next`), sharing login, device binding and Connector settings with Stable/Beta and other Next Profiles. Enablement remains per Profile; switching Profiles stops the previous Host and its remote connection. Existing Next-generated per-Profile state overrides are removed on the next Host start. Old state directories are retained without merging credentials; users who only signed in to the former isolated store may need to sign in again. AA's shared-state ownership checks still apply when multiple editions run concurrently.
- **Desktop tools:** open the data/Profile/log directories, reload the interface, open developer tools, export diagnostics, and open a macOS/Windows terminal with this installation’s `dsh`, `pnpm` and Electron-backed `node`. The terminal selects the original Profile even while the main app is in safe mode.

Markets, remote control and Computer Use appear above the ordinary plugin list, aligned to its content width. Remote control and Computer Use stack vertically, with settings gears to the left of their switches. The markets and remote bundle no longer appear again as ordinary plugin cards. These controls still use the official manager and persist in the current Profile; an existing Profile with both markets active asks the user to choose one. Bundle plugins installed by either market remain in the ordinary list for enablement, disablement and removal. dshmarket’s own plugin-disable behavior is unchanged. Existing choices migrate once from `desktop-next.features.json` into `package.json`; subsequent starts respect the official manager.

Sidebar extension entries reuse the original Desktop footer layout: entries stack vertically above Settings, with bounded scrolling to preserve the workspace list.

**Automation tasks** appears in the official Plugins group with upstream artwork, its experimental badge, the native enable switch, and component details. It is optional and disabled by default. Next preserves existing Schedule choices and their legacy Profile migration; it adds no separate Scheduled Tasks card.

### Browser and LAN access

Browser access is disabled by default. Enabling local access provides an authenticated loopback login link; enabling LAN access adds an HTTPS/WSS edge while the Host stays bound to `127.0.0.1`. Ports default to `0` (automatic). Access toggles do not restart the Host. Disabling browser access also disconnects existing browser WebSockets while preserving native streams and running tasks. Port changes require a Host restart. LAN addresses are sampled at startup; restart after a network change.

The settings page displays the complete local login URL and a separate HTTPS login URL for every LAN address, including the browser `token`. Each row opens or copies that exact URL. The login links are read through sender-validated native IPC and kept out of general runtime state and diagnostics. The page can also export the installation’s public CA certificate. Trust that certificate on the other device after comparing its SHA-256 fingerprint. Login links grant access and should only be shared with trusted devices. The CA private key is sealed with OS-backed storage; if secure storage or a suitable LAN address is unavailable, LAN HTTPS stays closed and the UI shows the failure. Native renderer credentials are never copied into these links and are stripped at the LAN edge.

### Native permissions and Computer Use

The gear beside Computer Use and **Settings → Desktop settings → Permissions** open an in-app permission dialog built with the official Modal, Button and StateDot components. It shows screen-recording, macOS Accessibility and microphone status. Opening the dialog only queries permissions. A user click requests OS consent or opens the corresponding system privacy pane. On macOS, changes made in System Settings may require restarting the application. macOS keeps no undecided state for screen recording or Accessibility: both read as not granted until the grant exists and stay requestable, a screen request being the first capture attempt that prompts; the dialog notes that macOS reopens the application once screen recording is enabled, and that an Accessibility entry System Settings still shows enabled belongs to an earlier build's signature and must be removed and added again. Windows microphone restrictions link to Windows privacy settings; unsupported status APIs report `unknown`, never a fabricated grant.

Next provides the `desktopPermissions` Cordis service to native client plugins and Host plugins. Import its types from `dsh-desktop-next/permissions` and inject `desktopPermissions`. Ordinary browser clients do not receive this service. Its methods are `query(permission)`, `request(permission)` and `openSettings(permission)`, where permission is `microphone`, `screen` or `accessibility`. Results include `status`, `canRequest` and `canOpenSettings`.

```ts
import type { Context } from '@deepseek-ai/cordis'
import type {} from 'dsh-desktop-next/permissions'

export const inject = ['desktopPermissions']

// Call directly from the native client plugin's Record button.
export async function record(ctx: Context) {
  const state = await ctx.desktopPermissions.request('microphone')
  if (state.status === 'denied' || state.status === 'restricted') return
  const stream = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({ audio: true })
  // Pass the stream to the recorder; stop every track when recording ends.
  return stream
}
```

Client requests require an active user gesture and the owning foreground window. Host requests cannot impersonate a user gesture: they reveal the permission dialog in the main window and return the current OS state, so the plugin must recheck after the user authorizes. Native settings requests made before the client mounts are retained for delivery. Host IPC uses correlated, bounded requests and rejects pending work on teardown. Permission status is always read again from the OS.

Screen sharing uses `navigator.mediaDevices.getDisplayMedia({ video: true, audio: false })` directly from the user's Share button. On macOS 15 and later, Electron uses the system picker; other systems use a native source-selection menu. No source is selected automatically. Per-capture system-picker consent can differ from the global screen-recording grant. The permission service does not record media, and screen sharing does not grant computer input control. Packaged Next retains its product-specific `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and signs the main application and Helpers directly with the pinned upstream `apps/desktop/scripts/macos-entitlements.plist`. Voice input uses Chromium/macOS recording consent through `getUserMedia`; the voice plugin has no separate permission button.

The official `@deepseek-ai/dsh-experimental-computer-use-cua-driver-native@0.1.6-alpha.2` provider is bundled and **disabled by default**. Use the Computer Use section at the top of **Plugins** to enable it and read its live loading status. This entry uses the official Plugins slot, switch and plugin manager; its Profile row ID is `computer-use-cua-driver-native`. The shared `computer-use` registry is already provided. Tools and screenshots use existing conversation tool cards and image attachments; screenshot understanding requires a model route declaring image input. The gear to the left of the switch opens the permission dialog.

The version-scoped Yarn patch at `patches/dsh-experimental-computer-use-cua-driver-native@0.1.6-alpha.2.patch` routes `check_permissions` through `desktopPermissions` when available. `prompt: true` reveals the permission dialog for missing grants, then the driver performs a read-only check with `prompt: false`. The driver remains the authority for its own actual permission status; no grant is inferred from the Desktop response. Without the Desktop service, the provider retains upstream behavior. The pinned `@trycua/cua-driver@0.28.0` binary, operation tools, image handling and shutdown ownership are unchanged. Only one provider can register, but that does not serialize concurrent Sessions operating the same desktop.

Unit tests exercise the installed patched provider with a fake native SDK. The optional native activation check requires a supported SDK platform, loads and shuts down the real provider, and sends no input or screenshots:

```sh
corepack yarn workspace dsh-desktop-next verify:host --computer-use
```

The optional `verify:window-controls --computer-use` smoke also enables and disables the real provider through the official frontend in headless Chromium, without calling its computer tools. Native OS consent and actual computer actions still need manual acceptance.

### Recovery

The independent recovery assistant shows the startup error and recent logs even if no Host is running. It offers retry, Profile switching, diagnostics, safe mode, repair, rollback and Quit. Restart in Recovery Mode from the Settings header fully stops the background service before relaunching directly into this assistant. The current Profile and plugins are not loaded until Start or retry is selected.

Recovery opened at startup follows the operating system's preferred language order, choosing the first supported Chinese or English language. It does not need a running Host to select its language. Once the main interface is available, native controls continue to follow the language selected in Settings.

- **Safe mode** starts the official interface in a separate temporary home with only shipped bundles, no original credentials, and remote control, Market and browser access disabled. Original data and configuration remain untouched. Leaving safe mode returns to the original Profile and removes the temporary home; work created in that temporary environment is not retained.
- **Profile repair** backs up the manifest, Profile patch and feature switches before restoring built-in bundles and disabling third-party activation, remote control and Market. A malformed `package.json` can be repaired. Installed plugin files, shared sessions and credentials are retained.
- **Profile rollback** restores the most recent successful Host-start configuration after backing up the current files and verifying the backup checksums. It covers `package.json`, `cordis.patch.yml` and Next feature switches, not installed plugin versions or shared data.
- **Global patch repair** separately backs up and disables the home-level `cordis.patch.yml`; this affects all Next Profiles. Profile repair never silently changes that patch.

Backups stay under `home/recovery/`. Diagnostics export a bounded JSON report with versions, state and redacted logs, without reading session or credential files. Logs can still contain local paths and plugin output; inspect the report before sharing. Local desktop logs are bounded to 128 KiB at `home/logs/desktop-next.log`. Desktop preferences live independently of Host settings in `home/desktop-preferences.json`.

Development and packaged builds default to `~/.dsh`, sharing Profiles and data with Stable; Next's selected Profile, Desktop preferences and related settings retain their own file names. The former `DSH NEXT/home` below the system application-data directory retains only the saved data-directory selection, so existing manual choices continue to work. Set `DSH_DESKTOP_NEXT_HOME` to an absolute path to choose a dedicated directory. Next does not select its home from the existing `DSH_HOME`. Factory reset still affects the entire current data directory, including data shared with Stable.

Ordinary Web Profiles do not declare `dsh-desktop-next` in `package.json`; Next supplies its capability only in its own Host startup and configuration recomposition. An older Next Profile has that historical bundle entry removed after its manifest is backed up, so Stable or the CLI will not load Next capabilities when opening the same Profile.

## Architecture and provenance

```text
Official Web frontend + official basic Desktop presentation
                        |  dsh-app://app
                 Next Electron main
                        |  authenticated HTTP / WebSocket
                 Electron Node-mode Host
                        |  upstream shared runProfile
                 Official Web bundles + Next bundle
                        |- Community Market
                        |- dshmarket
                        `- Agents Anywhere bridge
```

Alpha.2 replaced alpha.1's portless pipes with WebServer. This package uses the real upstream WebServer rather than simulating HTTP routes. The Host binds only to `127.0.0.1`, with an OS-assigned port by default so other editions can run concurrently. A separate optional TLS edge owns LAN ingress. Main retains Host cookies and a fresh native capability for each Host generation; ordinary HTTP and WebSocket requests are denied while browser access is off. Electron remains pinned to 44.7.0 for compatibility with the upstream native modules. Before forwarding a Host request, the main process attaches its native capability only to requests from the owned main frame at `dsh-app://app`, stripping that marker from other destinations and redirects. Native fetches may omit the HTTP `Origin` header. Market requests also require Host authentication, and mutations retain their translated loopback origin checks.

The main interface consumes official frontend artifacts without copying chat, settings, or plugin-manager pages. macOS window material, platform markers, the Windows caption menu, and native theme synchronization follow the official implementation. Editable areas in the main and shell windows show the official right-click editing menu: Undo, Redo, Cut, Copy, Paste, and Select All without shortcut labels, availability from Chromium, Copy alone for selected read-only text, and Windows labels in the current application language. The Windows caption buttons are the exception: their fill stays transparent and only their symbols follow the theme, so they always show whatever the page paints beneath them, including the official full-window onboarding and sign-in surfaces. Next contributes its Desktop section through `settings.section` and header shortcuts through `settings.action`. The Desktop section directly reuses `dsh-plugin-desktop-beta`'s `DesktopSettingsSection`, header actions and stylesheet. Recovery and Profile windows reuse its native React pages, frame and UI components. Next supplies state and command adapters, and capability options hide unsupported features; it does not maintain a second copy of those pages. Shared component changes are mirrored to Stable while preserving both editions' defaults. The application preload also installs the official `__DSH_HOST_PATHS__` bridge over Electron's `webUtils`: dropped, picked, and pasted files and folders with a real path enter the composer as `@path` references instead of uploads, and the official composer accepts dropped folders only when this bridge exists. Narrow sender-validated IPC exposes only named native actions. Ordinary browsers receive no native Desktop bridge. Adding a workspace in the main window opens the system folder dialog (Finder on macOS, Explorer on Windows) exactly as upstream Desktop does: Next hands its sampled LAN addresses to the Host as trusted authorities so LAN access can be switched on without a Host restart, which makes upstream's adaptive directory picker mount the in-app browsing panel, so Next's client bundle shadows that occupant in the Desktop window with a renderless driver over the preload bridge. Ordinary browsers reached through local or LAN access keep the panel the Host mounted.

Next contributes an application-owned profile layer at runtime; its recomposition hook keeps the layer active through shared plugin-manager operations and HMR without adding it to the shared Profile manifest. Version-scoped patches read `dsh.optionalBundles` and `dsh.exclusiveBundles` from the installation manifest and add `plugins.overview` and `plugins.bundle.hidden` slots to the published plugin-manager UI. Next uses these slots for the top controls and to omit duplicate bundle cards; installations without an exclusive group keep the original manager behavior. The dshmarket package runner uses the official `runPluginCommand` operation with Next’s Profile, installation anchor and bundled pnpm; it does not require pnpm on the system PATH. Development startup creates one managed link for Next itself under `home/profiles/node_modules`; alpha.2 runtime resolution owns all other dependency fallbacks. All upstream runtime dependencies come from published packages, without source links into or edits to `deepseek-harness/`.

[upstream-reference.json](upstream-reference.json) records the reference commit and original hashes of copied files; [LICENSE.upstream](LICENSE.upstream) retains the original license.

## Current limits

Packaging entry points and the Next update client are implemented. Releases still require producing and validating platform artifacts and configuring the online Next channel. Stable/Beta data migration is not provided. Our enhanced/extended window modes remain deferred. An unpublished Next update channel is reported as unavailable; Next never installs a Stable/Beta package. Enhanced window modes remain hidden. Headless Node/Electron checks do not qualify cross-platform installers or visual behavior.

## Packaging and updates

The product version is `2.0.20-next`. Run from the repository root:

```sh
corepack yarn package:dir:next
corepack yarn dist:mac-smoke:next
corepack yarn dist:mac:next
corepack yarn dist:win:next
```

Packaging reuses Beta's directory builds, universal macOS DMGs, signing/notarization preflight and Windows x64 NSIS flow, including its unsigned Windows build policy. Like upstream Desktop, the application is archived into `app.asar`; native modules, executables, nested bundles, the bundled pnpm, the AA bridge's Connector project, the Node shims and the icon assets are unpacked
